plans.title: 21 Days in John
plans.description: Read one chapter a day through John's Gospel.
plans.purpose: To help you stay with one Bible book long enough to notice its flow and message.
plans.bestFor: Slow book-by-book reading
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: 21 readings beginning with John 1 and ending with John 21.
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

devotional.title: The Word became flesh
devotional.body: John opens by showing that Jesus is eternal, divine, Creator, Light, and the Word made flesh. The chapter does not present Jesus as merely a teacher; He is the Son who reveals the Father and brings grace and truth.

days.reflectionPrompt: Which truth about Jesus in John 1 most needs to shape your worship today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me receive Your light, grace, and truth.
days.context: John opens with a theological prologue before the narrative ministry begins. The chapter presents Jesus as the eternal Word, Creator, Light, and Son who reveals the Father. John immediately ties belief, witness, grace, truth, and the incarnation together.

devotional.title: Glory revealed in signs
devotional.body: Jesus' first sign at Cana and His cleansing of the temple both reveal His authority. He brings joy, fulfills what old symbols pointed toward, and claims the right to reorder worship around Himself.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need Jesus to reorder shallow religion into true worship?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, purify my worship and teach me to trust Your glory.
days.context: John 2 begins the book's signs at Cana and then moves to Jesus cleansing the temple in Jerusalem. Both scenes reveal Jesus' glory and authority over old covenant symbols. The chapter points forward to His death and resurrection as the true temple.

devotional.title: Born from above
devotional.body: Nicodemus learns that religious knowledge cannot replace new birth. The Son is lifted up so that believing sinners may receive eternal life, not condemnation, through God's love.

days.reflectionPrompt: What would it mean to receive salvation as new birth rather than self-improvement?
days.prayerPrompt: Father, thank You for loving the world by giving Your Son.
days.context: Nicodemus comes to Jesus as a respected Jewish teacher, yet Jesus says entrance into God's kingdom requires birth from above. The chapter joins new birth, the Spirit's work, the lifted-up Son, and God's love for the world. Salvation is received by faith, not status.

devotional.title: Living water for outsiders
devotional.body: Jesus meets a Samaritan woman with truth and mercy. He exposes thirst, offers living water, and teaches that true worship is in spirit and truth.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where are you trying to satisfy thirst apart from Christ?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, give me living water and make me a truthful worshiper.
days.context: Jesus crosses social and religious boundaries by speaking with a Samaritan woman. The chapter contrasts old hostilities with the gift of living water and worship in spirit and truth. Her witness also prepares a wider Samaritan response to Jesus as Savior.

devotional.title: The Son gives life
devotional.body: Jesus heals on the Sabbath and teaches that the Son does the Father's work, gives life, and will raise the dead. The chapter presses readers to honor the Son as they honor the Father.

days.reflectionPrompt: How might Jesus' authority to give life strengthen your trust in Him today?
days.prayerPrompt: Father, help me honor the Son and hear His voice with faith.
days.context: A Sabbath healing leads into one of John's major discourses about Jesus' authority. Jesus presents His work as the Father's work and speaks of life, judgment, resurrection, and witness. The issue is not merely healing, but whether people honor the Son.

devotional.title: The bread of life
devotional.body: After feeding the crowd, Jesus teaches that He Himself is the true bread from heaven. He does not merely give gifts; He gives Himself for the life of the world.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where are you seeking satisfaction without coming to Christ Himself?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, feed my soul with Yourself, the bread of life.
days.context: John 6 follows the feeding of the crowd and Jesus walking on the sea with the Bread of Life discourse. The crowd wants provision, but Jesus presses deeper toward faith in Himself. The chapter separates temporary satisfaction from receiving the Son given for life.

devotional.title: Thirst and division
devotional.body: At the feast, Jesus calls the thirsty to come to Him and drink while crowds divide over His identity. His words expose whether people judge by appearance or receive Him by faith.

days.reflectionPrompt: What thirst or confusion does Jesus invite you to bring to Him?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, teach me to come to You and receive the Spirit's life.
days.context: Jesus teaches during the Feast of Tabernacles while public opinion about Him is divided. The feast setting highlights water, light, and hope, and Jesus invites the thirsty to come to Him. The chapter shows how His identity exposes shallow judgments.

devotional.title: Truth that sets free
devotional.body: Jesus confronts false confidence and offers freedom through abiding in His word. True freedom is not self-rule; it is rescue from sin through the Son.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need freedom that comes from abiding in Jesus' word?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, keep me in Your truth and set me free from sin's lies.
days.context: John 8 continues the conflict over Jesus' identity, testimony, and relationship to the Father. Jesus calls hearers to abide in His word and tells them true freedom comes through the Son. The chapter confronts false confidence while offering truth that liberates.

devotional.title: Sight for the blind
devotional.body: Jesus gives sight to a man born blind while religious leaders reveal spiritual blindness. The sign asks whether we will truly see and worship the Son of Man.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where might pride keep you from seeing what Jesus is showing?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, open my eyes and lead me to worship You.
days.context: Jesus heals a man born blind, and the sign becomes a trial of spiritual sight. The healed man moves toward clearer confession while the religious leaders harden in resistance. John uses physical sight to reveal the deeper question of recognizing Jesus.

devotional.title: The good Shepherd
devotional.body: Jesus is the door and the good Shepherd who knows His sheep, lays down His life, and gives eternal life. His care is personal, costly, and secure.

days.reflectionPrompt: Which promise of the Shepherd most steadies you today?
days.prayerPrompt: Good Shepherd, help me hear Your voice and rest in Your care.
days.context: Jesus speaks as the door and the good Shepherd in contrast to false or harmful shepherds. The chapter draws on Old Testament shepherd imagery and emphasizes His knowledge, protection, sacrifice, and authority. His sheep are secure because He gives His life.

devotional.title: Resurrection and tears
devotional.body: At Lazarus' tomb, Jesus weeps and then reveals Himself as the resurrection and the life. He meets grief with compassion and hope that is stronger than death.

days.reflectionPrompt: What grief needs both the tears and power of Jesus?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, meet me in sorrow and keep my hope in Your life.
days.context: The raising of Lazarus stands near the turning point toward Jesus' death. Jesus delays, weeps, speaks with Martha, and reveals Himself as resurrection and life before raising Lazarus. The sign offers real hope without minimizing grief or death.

devotional.title: The hour has come
devotional.body: Mary's worship, the crowd's praise, and Jesus' teaching all move toward His hour. The grain of wheat must die to bear fruit, pointing to the cross.

days.reflectionPrompt: How might Jesus' path of self-giving love shape your response to Him today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me follow You in humble, fruitful obedience.
days.context: John 12 closes the public ministry as Jesus' hour approaches. Mary's anointing, the triumphal entry, and Jesus' teaching about the grain of wheat all point toward the cross. Glory in John is revealed through Jesus' self-giving death.

devotional.title: Love with a towel
devotional.body: Jesus washes His disciples' feet and commands them to love one another. His authority is expressed in humble service, and His people are marked by His love.

days.reflectionPrompt: Who is Jesus calling you to serve with humble love?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, wash me, humble me, and make Your love visible in me.
days.context: John 13 begins the farewell section on the night before the cross. Jesus washes His disciples' feet, identifies betrayal, and gives the new command to love one another. The scene roots Christian service and love in His own humble, cleansing work.

devotional.title: The way to the Father
devotional.body: Jesus comforts troubled disciples by promising the Father's house, the Spirit, and His peace. He is not one way among many; He is the way, the truth, and the life.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where does your troubled heart need Christ's peace and promise?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, keep my heart trusting You as the way to the Father.
days.context: Jesus speaks to troubled disciples during the farewell discourse. He comforts them with the Father's house, His unique way to the Father, the coming Spirit, and His peace. The chapter prepares believers for His departure without leaving them orphaned.

devotional.title: Abide and bear fruit
devotional.body: Jesus describes Himself as the true vine and calls His disciples to abide in Him. Fruitful life comes from remaining in His love, not from detached effort.

days.reflectionPrompt: What would abiding in Christ look like in one ordinary part of today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, keep me near You so my life bears fruit that honors You.
days.context: John 15 continues the farewell discourse with the image of the true vine. Jesus calls His disciples to remain in Him, receive His words, keep His commands, and bear fruit in love. Fruitfulness is rooted in union and dependence, not detached effort.

devotional.title: Sorrow turned to joy
devotional.body: Jesus prepares His disciples for grief, opposition, and the Spirit's help. Their sorrow will be real, but it will not be final because He overcomes the world.

days.reflectionPrompt: What sorrow or fear needs to be held under Jesus' victory?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, give me courage because You have overcome the world.
days.context: Jesus prepares His disciples for sorrow, opposition, and the Spirit's witness after His departure. He does not deny their grief, but promises the Spirit's help and joy beyond the coming anguish. The chapter ends with courage grounded in His victory.

devotional.title: Jesus prays for His people
devotional.body: Jesus prays for His disciples and for those who will believe through their word. He asks for protection, holiness, unity, and that His people would behold His glory.

days.reflectionPrompt: Which part of Jesus' prayer gives you assurance or direction today?
days.prayerPrompt: Father, sanctify me in Your truth and keep me in the love of Christ.
days.context: John 17 records Jesus' prayer before His arrest. He prays for the Father's glory, His disciples' protection and holiness, and future believers' unity and witness. The prayer lets readers hear what Jesus desires for His people before the cross.

devotional.title: The King on trial
devotional.body: Jesus is arrested and questioned while Peter denies Him. Even in apparent weakness, Jesus stands as the true King whose kingdom is not from this world.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need courage to confess Christ rather than shrink back?
days.prayerPrompt: King Jesus, strengthen my loyalty when pressure exposes my weakness.
days.context: John 18 moves from Jesus' arrest to questioning before Jewish leaders and Pilate. Peter's denial is set beside Jesus' steady testimony about His kingdom. The chapter shows the true King apparently judged by human powers while remaining in control.

devotional.title: It is finished
devotional.body: John shows Jesus crucified as the true King and sacrificial Savior. His finished work is not defeat; it is the completion of the saving work the Father gave Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What burden do you need to bring under Jesus' words, 'It is finished'?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, thank You for finishing the work of salvation at the cross.
days.context: John 19 presents the crucifixion with repeated emphasis on Jesus as King and on Scripture being fulfilled. His death is not accidental failure but the completion of the work given by the Father. The chapter invites faith in the finished saving work of Christ.

devotional.title: Believe and have life
devotional.body: The risen Jesus appears to Mary, the disciples, and Thomas. John states his purpose clearly: these things are written so readers may believe and have life in Jesus' name.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does the risen Christ invite you from doubt or grief into faith?
days.prayerPrompt: Risen Lord, deepen my faith and life in Your name.
days.context: John 20 narrates the empty tomb and resurrection appearances to Mary, the disciples, and Thomas. The chapter names John's purpose: written testimony so readers may believe Jesus is the Christ and have life in His name. Doubt is met by the risen Lord.

devotional.title: Restored to follow
devotional.body: Jesus meets failed disciples with breakfast, restoration, and a renewed call to follow. Peter's failure is not the end of his discipleship because Jesus restores and sends him.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to receive Jesus' restoration and follow Him again?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, restore my love and help me follow You faithfully.
days.context: John 21 functions as an epilogue after the stated purpose of the Gospel. Jesus provides for His disciples, restores Peter after denial, and renews the call to follow. The chapter shows that resurrection grace sends restored disciples into faithful service.

plans.title: Romans in 16 Days
plans.description: Move slowly through Paul's letter one chapter at a time.
plans.purpose: To help you stay with one Bible book long enough to notice its flow and message.
plans.bestFor: Slow book-by-book reading
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: 16 readings beginning with Romans 1 and ending with Romans 16.
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

devotional.title: The gospel of God
devotional.body: Paul introduces the gospel as God's promised good news about His Son. Human sin is serious, but the letter begins with the righteousness of God revealed through faith.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does beginning with God's good news about His Son steady the way you read Romans?
days.prayerPrompt: Father, help me receive the gospel as Your good news about Your Son.
days.context: Paul writes to believers in Rome and begins by announcing the gospel promised in Scripture concerning God's Son. The chapter introduces key themes: faith, righteousness, Gentile mission, and humanity's refusal to honor God. It sets the need for salvation before explaining it.

devotional.title: Judgment and true obedience
devotional.body: Paul warns religious and moral people not to hide behind comparison. God's judgment is truthful, impartial, and concerned with reality rather than outward labels.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where are you tempted to rely on comparison instead of honest repentance?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, make my faith sincere from the heart, not merely outward.
days.context: Romans 2 turns from obvious Gentile sin toward moral and religious self-confidence. Paul warns that possession of God's law or outward religious markers cannot replace obedient reality before God. The argument exposes every basis for boasting before the impartial Judge.

devotional.title: Righteousness through faith
devotional.body: Paul gathers all people under sin, then announces righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ. Grace is not vague kindness; it comes through Christ's redeeming blood.

days.reflectionPrompt: What makes grace necessary and secure in this chapter?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, thank You for redemption and righteousness received by faith.
days.context: Romans 3 draws Jew and Gentile alike under sin before announcing God's righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ. Paul holds together human guilt, God's justice, redemption, and grace. The chapter is central to Romans because it shows why the gospel is necessary and secure.

devotional.title: Faith counted as righteousness
devotional.body: Abraham is Paul’s example that righteousness is received by faith, not achieved by works. God's promise rests on grace so that it may be certain.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to trust promise rather than performance?
days.prayerPrompt: God of promise, strengthen my faith in what You have done.
days.context: Paul uses Abraham and David to show that justification has always rested on faith rather than works. Abraham is counted righteous before circumcision, so the promise can embrace Gentiles as well as Jews. The chapter anchors Christian assurance in God's gracious promise.

devotional.title: Peace with God
devotional.body: Because believers are justified by faith, they have peace with God through Christ. Adam's trespass brought death, but Christ's obedience brings grace and life.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Christ's work give you peace that your performance cannot create?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me stand in the grace You have given.
days.context: Romans 5 follows justification by describing peace with God, hope in suffering, and God's love shown in Christ's death. Paul then contrasts Adam and Christ as two representative heads. The chapter shows grace reigning where sin and death once ruled.

devotional.title: Dead to sin, alive to God
devotional.body: Paul rejects the idea that grace excuses sin. Union with Christ means believers have died to sin and are called to walk in newness of life.

days.reflectionPrompt: What old pattern needs to be treated as no longer your master?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, help me live as one alive to You in Christ Jesus.
days.context: After celebrating grace, Paul answers the objection that grace might encourage sin. Paul connects baptism into Christ with His death and resurrection. The chapter calls believers to live from their new identity: dead to sin and alive to God.

devotional.title: The law and the struggle
devotional.body: Paul shows the goodness of God's law and the deep struggle of sin within. The cry for rescue prepares the way for the hope of Christ and the Spirit.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you feel the need for rescue rather than mere resolution?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, rescue me from sin's power and teach me dependence.
days.context: Romans 7 explains the law's goodness while exposing sin's deep power. Paul shows that God's commandment is not the problem; sin seizes the commandment and produces death. The chapter's cry for rescue prepares readers for life in the Spirit in Romans 8.

devotional.title: Life in the Spirit
devotional.body: Romans 8 gathers assurance, Spirit-led life, suffering, hope, prayer, and God's unbreakable love. No condemnation leads to no separation in Christ.

days.reflectionPrompt: Which promise in Romans 8 most strengthens your assurance today?
days.prayerPrompt: Father, help me walk by the Spirit and rest in Your inseparable love.
days.context: Romans 8 is the summit of Paul's argument about life in Christ and the Spirit. It moves from no condemnation to adoption, suffering, future glory, Spirit-led prayer, and inseparable love. Assurance is grounded in God's action in Christ, not in denial of hardship.

devotional.title: Mercy and God's purpose
devotional.body: Paul grieves Israel's unbelief while defending God's freedom and mercy. The chapter calls for humility before God's purposes rather than presumption.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does this chapter humble both pride and despair?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, keep me humble before Your mercy and faithful in prayer for others.
days.context: Romans 9 begins Paul's three-chapter reflection on Israel, God's promises, and Gentile inclusion. Paul grieves Israel's unbelief while insisting that God's word has not failed. The chapter must be read with humility, lament, and confidence in God's mercy.

devotional.title: Christ and the preached word
devotional.body: Paul longs for Israel's salvation and shows that righteousness is not far away in Christ. Faith comes through hearing the word of Christ.

days.reflectionPrompt: Who needs your prayer that they would hear and respond to Christ?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, send Your word with power and make me faithful to confess Christ.
days.context: Romans 10 continues Paul's concern for Israel's salvation and contrasts zeal without knowledge with righteousness in Christ. Paul emphasizes confession, faith, preaching, and hearing the word of Christ. The chapter keeps mission and prayer tied to the gospel message.

devotional.title: Mercy for Jew and Gentile
devotional.body: Paul warns Gentile believers against arrogance and marvels at God's mercy. The chapter ends in worship before God's wisdom and ways.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need wonder instead of pride when thinking about salvation?
days.prayerPrompt: Oh the depth of Your wisdom, Lord. Keep me humble in Your mercy.
days.context: Romans 11 completes Paul's reflection on Israel and the nations. Gentile believers are warned against arrogance, Israel's stumbling is not treated as final, and all mercy leads to worship. The chapter ends by bowing before God's wisdom rather than explaining everything neatly.

devotional.title: Living sacrifice
devotional.body: The mercies of God lead to whole-life worship. Paul moves from grace to transformed minds, humble gifts, sincere love, patience, hospitality, and peace.

days.reflectionPrompt: Which mark of transformed life is the Spirit pressing on you today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, make my ordinary life an offering of worship to You.
days.context: Romans 12 begins the practical section with the mercies of God as the foundation for whole-life worship. Paul moves from renewed minds to humble use of gifts and sincere love. Christian obedience here is response to grace, not a way to earn it.

devotional.title: Love and wakefulness
devotional.body: Paul speaks about governing authorities, love as fulfilling the law, and living awake in light of the coming day. Christian ethics are shaped by love and hope.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where does love need to become concrete rather than merely intended?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, help me walk honorably in love as one who belongs to the day.
days.context: Romans 13 applies gospel-shaped life to public order, neighbor love, and alert holiness. Paul speaks of governing authorities, then summarizes the law through love. The chapter closes with urgency because believers live in light of the coming day.

devotional.title: Welcome without contempt
devotional.body: Paul teaches believers to welcome one another amid disputable matters. Love limits freedom for the sake of a brother or sister for whom Christ died.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to trade contempt or judgment for patient love?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, teach me to honor Your people with humility and care.
days.context: Romans 14 addresses tensions among believers over disputable matters such as food and special days. Paul calls the church away from contempt and judgment toward welcome, conscience, and love. Freedom is real, but it is governed by Christ's lordship and care for others.

devotional.title: Hope and mission
devotional.body: Paul calls strong believers to bear with the weak, points to Christ's servant-hearted welcome, and looks outward to gospel mission among the nations.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Christ's welcome reshape the way you welcome others?
days.prayerPrompt: God of hope, fill me with joy and peace in believing.
days.context: Romans 15 continues the call for the strong to bear with the weak and roots welcome in Christ's own welcome. Paul also gathers Scripture to show God's mercy reaching the nations. The chapter moves naturally from church unity to gospel mission.

devotional.title: Grace among real people
devotional.body: Romans ends with names, greetings, warnings, and praise. The gospel creates a real community of servants, households, coworkers, and faithful witnesses.

days.reflectionPrompt: Who has helped your faith, and who can you encourage in the Lord?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, thank You for Your people. Make me faithful in ordinary service.
days.context: Romans 16 is more than an appendix; it reveals the network of real people shaped by the gospel. Paul greets women and men, households, coworkers, and servants while warning against division. The letter ends with praise to the God who establishes His people through the gospel.

plans.title: Psalms for Prayer
plans.description: Twenty-one Psalms chosen to shape prayer, trust, confession, and worship.
plans.purpose: To help you turn Scripture into prayer, trust, worship, and honest dependence on God.
plans.bestFor: Prayer, devotional reading, and reflection
plans.estimatedTime: 10-15 minutes
plans.coverage: 21 readings beginning with Psalm 1-8 and ending with Psalm 144-150.
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

devotional.title: Prayer begins with delight
devotional.body: The Psalms open by contrasting the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked, then move through trouble, trust, and praise. Prayer begins with delight in God's instruction and honest dependence on His care.

days.reflectionPrompt: Which desire, fear, confession, or praise from these Psalms gives words to your prayer today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, root my life in Your word and teach me to pray honestly.
days.context: The Psalter opens by setting the way of the righteous beside the way of the wicked, then moves quickly into kingship, lament, and trust. These early prayers introduce delight in God's instruction, opposition to God's rule, and confidence that the Lord hears.

devotional.title: Refuge and trust
devotional.body: These Psalms bring enemies, injustice, lament, and confidence before the Lord. They teach that prayer can name danger while taking refuge in God's faithful rule.

days.reflectionPrompt: Which line helps you bring fear or injustice to the Lord today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, be my refuge and keep my heart trusting You.
days.context: This section includes individual and communal prayers that name injustice, danger, corruption, and refuge. Davidic laments and songs of trust sit beside confidence in the Lord's righteous judgment. Prayer here learns to bring fear and public wrong before God.

devotional.title: The King and Shepherd
devotional.body: David prays for protection, celebrates deliverance, hears creation declare God's glory, and sings of the Lord as Shepherd and King. Prayer becomes both need and worship.

days.reflectionPrompt: How do these Psalms move you from request to worship?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, shepherd me, search me, and reign over my heart.
days.context: These Psalms move from pleas for protection to rescue, creation's witness, royal strength, shepherd care, and the King of glory. Several are Davidic and teach prayer that is both personal and public. Need, worship, and kingship belong together.

devotional.title: Teach me Your ways
devotional.body: These Psalms repeatedly ask for guidance, forgiveness, protection, and courage. They train believers to bring shame, fear, waiting, and trust into God's presence.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to pray, 'Teach me Your paths'?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, guide me in Your truth and keep me waiting with courage.
days.context: Davidic prayers dominate this section, often asking for guidance, forgiveness, protection, and deliverance. The language of waiting, shame, enemies, and trust gives shape to honest dependence. Prayer asks the Lord to teach His paths while holding trouble before Him.

devotional.title: Confession and mercy
devotional.body: This section gives words for confession, forgiveness, praise, and physical or emotional distress. The Lord's mercy is not thin; it meets real guilt and real weakness.

days.reflectionPrompt: What needs to be confessed or received under God's steadfast love?
days.prayerPrompt: Merciful Lord, forgive, restore, and surround me with Your steadfast love.
days.context: These Psalms include confession, instruction, praise, and prayers from weakness or distress. They do not separate spiritual guilt from embodied suffering too neatly, but bring the whole person before God. Mercy, forgiveness, and steadfast love remain central.

devotional.title: Hope while waiting
devotional.body: These Psalms hold mortality, waiting, sorrow, rescue, and royal hope together. They teach patience that looks beyond self to the Lord's faithful deliverance.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to wait without losing hope in the Lord?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, put a new song in my mouth and keep my hope in You.
days.context: This section brings mortality, waiting, lament, deliverance, and royal hope into prayer. Several Psalms wrestle with frailty and delayed rescue, while others praise God's help and the king's beauty. Hope is learned while still waiting on the Lord.

devotional.title: God is our refuge
devotional.body: Psalm 46 anchors this section in God's presence amid shaking. The following Psalms praise His kingship and confront evil, deceit, and misplaced confidence.

days.reflectionPrompt: What false security needs to give way to God as refuge?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Almighty, be my refuge and teach me to rest under Your reign.
days.context: Psalm 46 begins this range with Zion confidence: creation shakes and nations rage, yet the Lord of hosts is with His people. The surrounding Psalms praise God's kingship and confront deceit, violence, and misplaced security. Refuge is found in God's reign.

devotional.title: Prayer under pressure
devotional.body: These Psalms pray amid corruption, betrayal, danger, and pursuit. They show that faith can speak plainly to God when human help feels unreliable.

days.reflectionPrompt: What pressure do you need to bring to God without polishing the words?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, hear me under pressure and keep me faithful.
days.context: These Psalms include prayers about folly, betrayal, enemies, and danger, many linked to David's pressured seasons. They speak plainly about human evil without pretending the faithful are untouched. Prayer becomes a way to entrust threat and vindication to God.

devotional.title: Rescue and praise
devotional.body: This section moves from defeat and need to confidence, blessing, and praise. Prayer remembers that deliverance belongs to God and turns answered prayer into worship.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where has the Lord carried you, corrected you, or heard you?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, let Your rescue lead me into grateful praise.
days.context: This range moves through defeat, longing, confidence, blessing, and corporate praise. Some Psalms remember trouble and correction; others summon all the earth to worship. Prayer here turns need and deliverance into testimony before God and His people.

devotional.title: Blessing, justice, and nearness
devotional.body: These Psalms ask God to bless the nations, defend the needy, and steady the heart when the wicked prosper. Psalm 73 brings the believer back to the nearness of God.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to say, 'But as for me, it is good to be near God'?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, be my portion and steady my heart when life feels uneven.
days.context: These Psalms widen prayer toward the nations, justice for the needy, royal righteousness, and the struggle of seeing the wicked prosper. Psalm 73 resolves envy by entering God's presence. Blessing is meant to lead to worship, justice, and nearness to God.

devotional.title: Lament for God's people
devotional.body: These communal laments ask why devastation has come and plead for restoration. Prayer is not only individual; God's people grieve and hope together.

days.reflectionPrompt: What burden for God's people or the world do you need to bring before Him?
days.prayerPrompt: Shepherd of Israel, restore us and make Your face shine.
days.context: This section is heavy with communal lament after devastation among God's people. The prayers ask why, remember God's past acts, and plead for restoration. They show that biblical prayer can carry shared grief, public loss, and hope for God's face to shine again.

devotional.title: Listen and return
devotional.body: The Lord calls His people to listen, turn from idols, and seek justice. These Psalms also celebrate Zion as the place of God's dwelling and blessing.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where is God calling you to listen more deeply and return?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, free me from false worship and tune my heart to Your voice.
days.context: These Psalms call God's people to listen, remember, turn from idols, seek justice, and rejoice in Zion. Some speak with God's own covenant appeal, while others celebrate His dwelling with His people. Prayer includes both return and worship.

devotional.title: Darkness and reign
devotional.body: Psalm 88 gives one of Scripture's darkest prayers, while later Psalms proclaim the Lord's reign and justice. Faith can pray from darkness without abandoning God's throne.

days.reflectionPrompt: What lament can you bring to the reigning Lord today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, meet me in darkness and keep me trusting Your righteous rule.
days.context: Psalm 88 is one of Scripture's darkest laments, and the following Psalms answer darkness with covenant remembrance and the Lord's reign. This range does not rush grief into easy resolution. It teaches prayer that can speak from the depths while still addressing God.

devotional.title: Worship the King
devotional.body: These Psalms call creation and nations to worship the Lord as King. Praise includes reverence, joy, justice, holiness, and obedience.

days.reflectionPrompt: What reason for worship stands out most clearly in these Psalms?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, make my worship joyful, reverent, and obedient.
days.context: This section contains strong calls to worship the Lord as Creator, King, Judge, and holy ruler. The Psalms summon nations and creation, while also warning God's people not to harden their hearts. Praise and obedience are held together.

devotional.title: Steadfast love across generations
devotional.body: These Psalms move through affliction, forgiveness, human frailty, and God's enduring love. Prayer finds hope in the Lord whose years have no end.

days.reflectionPrompt: What weakness can you bring to the everlasting mercy of God?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, remember me with Your steadfast love and renew my praise.
days.context: These Psalms move from afflicted prayer to remembrance of God's enduring mercy, covenant love, and help for His people. Human life is frail, but the Lord's steadfast love spans generations. Prayer here holds weakness within God's larger faithfulness.

devotional.title: Justice, Messiah, and glory
devotional.body: These Psalms cry for justice, speak of the Lord's chosen King and Priest, and reject idols. Prayer learns to seek God's glory above human vengeance or false trust.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need God's justice and glory to reframe your response?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, not to us, but to Your name give glory.
days.context: This range includes hard prayers for justice, royal and priestly hope, praise for God's works, and rejection of idols. Psalm 110 is especially important for later messianic reading. The section teaches prayer to seek God's name and rule above human revenge or false trust.

devotional.title: Thanks and pilgrimage
devotional.body: These Psalms thank the Lord for rescue and then move into songs for the journey to worship. Prayer becomes gratitude, testimony, and longing for peace.

days.reflectionPrompt: What rescue or mercy should become thanksgiving today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, thank You for hearing me. Lead me in peace and worship.
days.context: These Psalms move from thanksgiving for rescue into the Songs of Ascents, prayers for pilgrims going up to worship. Gratitude, testimony, Jerusalem, peace, and dependence shape the section. Prayer becomes a journey toward worship with God's people.

devotional.title: Dependence on the journey
devotional.body: The pilgrim Psalms lift tired eyes to the Lord, remember His help, and ask for mercy. They form prayer for people who are still on the way.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to lift your eyes to the Lord rather than stare at the difficulty?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, have mercy and keep me walking with You.
days.context: These Songs of Ascents continue the pilgrim pattern with mercy, help, deliverance, and endurance under contempt or oppression. The prayers are short but communal and road-tested. They teach weary people to lift their eyes to the Lord while still on the way.

devotional.title: Waiting and steadfast love
devotional.body: These Psalms move from the depths to hope, unity, worship, and the repeated refrain of God's steadfast love. Waiting is held by mercy.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where might the Lord's steadfast love help you wait with hope rather than despair?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, from the depths I wait for You and trust Your unfailing mercy.
days.context: This range moves from the depths of confession to waiting hope, humble trust, unity, blessing, and repeated praise for steadfast love. The Psalms teach that mercy is not shallow optimism. Waiting is held by forgiveness and the Lord's enduring covenant love.

devotional.title: Exile, honesty, and rescue
devotional.body: These Psalms include the ache of exile, thanksgiving, searching prayer, and pleas for deliverance. They teach honest prayer that still turns toward God's faithful character.

days.reflectionPrompt: What hard emotion needs to be prayed honestly before the Lord?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, search me, lead me, and deliver me according to Your steadfast love.
days.context: These Psalms include exile's grief, thanksgiving, searching prayer, and pleas for rescue from enemies. Some language is raw and should not be flattened into private irritation. Prayer here brings hard memory, longing, and need before the faithful Lord.

devotional.title: Everything that has breath
devotional.body: The Psalter ends with rescue, kingdom praise, and a crescendo of hallelujah. Prayer that began with delight now gathers every breath into praise.

days.reflectionPrompt: How can praise become the final word over this season of prayer?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, let everything in me praise You with joy and faithfulness.
days.context: The Psalter closes with rescue, royal hope, creation praise, and a final crescendo of hallelujahs. These Psalms gather the whole book's movement from lament and trust into praise. The ending calls every breath to worship the Lord.

plans.title: Bible in 1 Year
plans.description: A simple chapter-by-chapter path through every book of the Bible.
plans.purpose: To build a steady year-long rhythm through the whole Bible while keeping each book within the larger story of creation, covenant, Christ, church, and new creation.
plans.bestFor: Readers who want a simple whole-Bible habit without jumping between testaments each day.
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–20 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: A chapter-by-chapter journey from Genesis to Revelation across one year.
plans.rhythm: Read the daily portion, notice where the current book sits in Scripture's story, pray briefly, then mark the day complete.

days.context: Genesis stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Genesis
devotional.body: Genesis belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Genesis begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Joshua show about the Lord's faithfulness in the middle of human faithfulness and failure?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, teach me to read history with humility, repentance, and trust in Your purposes.

plans.title: Bible in 1 Year Chronological
plans.description: Read the Bible in a broad historical flow over one year.
plans.purpose: To help you follow the Bible story in a roughly historical order from creation, the patriarchs, Israel, exile, Jesus, the church, and new creation.
plans.bestFor: Readers who want the storyline of Scripture to feel connected across the whole year.
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–20 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: A whole-Bible journey arranged in a broad chronological-style sequence.
plans.rhythm: Read the daily portion, notice where it fits in the story, pray, then mark the day complete.

days.context: Genesis stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Genesis
devotional.body: Genesis belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Genesis begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.

days.context: Job stands among Scripture's wisdom and worship books, where prayer, praise, lament, desire, suffering, limits, and practical discernment are brought before God. Read slowly, allowing the genre to shape worship and wisdom before immediate application.

devotional.title: Learning prayer and wisdom in Job
devotional.body: Job trains the heart as well as the mind. Read for worship, honest prayer, wisdom, limits, longing, and faithful living before God. Let the passage shape what you love, fear, ask, confess, and practice.

days.reflectionPrompt: What desire, prayer, or wisdom is Job forming in you today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, shape my heart with wisdom, worship, and honest prayer.

days.context: Joshua belongs to the historical books, where Israel's life in the land, leadership, worship, failure, judgment, and mercy unfold in real events. Read this book as part of God's covenant dealings rather than as isolated moral examples.

devotional.title: Entering Joshua
devotional.body: Joshua tells part of Israel's lived history with the Lord. Watch for faithfulness and failure, leadership and worship, judgment and mercy. These chapters are not merely examples to imitate or avoid; they show how God's purposes continue through real people and real consequences.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Joshua show about the Lord's faithfulness in the middle of human faithfulness and failure?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, teach me to read history with humility, repentance, and trust in Your purposes.

plans.bestFor: Readers who want a focused season of stronger whole-Bible momentum.
plans.estimatedTime: About 15–35 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: A path from Genesis 1-7 through Revelation 17-22, covering the whole Bible in arranged daily portions.
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Genesis stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Genesis
devotional.body: Genesis belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Genesis begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.

days.context: Joshua belongs to the historical books, where Israel's life in the land, leadership, worship, failure, judgment, and mercy unfold in real events. Read this book as part of God's covenant dealings rather than as isolated moral examples.

devotional.title: Entering Joshua
devotional.body: Joshua tells part of Israel's lived history with the Lord. Watch for faithfulness and failure, leadership and worship, judgment and mercy. These chapters are not merely examples to imitate or avoid; they show how God's purposes continue through real people and real consequences.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Joshua show about the Lord's faithfulness in the middle of human faithfulness and failure?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, teach me to read history with humility, repentance, and trust in Your purposes.

days.context: Job stands among Scripture's wisdom and worship books, where prayer, praise, lament, desire, suffering, limits, and practical discernment are brought before God. Read slowly, allowing the genre to shape worship and wisdom before immediate application.

devotional.title: Learning prayer and wisdom in Job
devotional.body: Job trains the heart as well as the mind. Read for worship, honest prayer, wisdom, limits, longing, and faithful living before God. Let the passage shape what you love, fear, ask, confess, and practice.

days.reflectionPrompt: What desire, prayer, or wisdom is Job forming in you today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, shape my heart with wisdom, worship, and honest prayer.

days.context: Isaiah belongs to the prophetic witness, where the Lord addresses covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, idolatry, judgment, mercy, and future hope. Read the opening section as God's word to His people before turning it into private prediction or general advice.

devotional.title: Listening to Isaiah
devotional.body: Isaiah speaks into covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, judgment, mercy, and hope. Prophetic books are not mainly prediction puzzles; they call God's people to hear His word, return to Him, and trust His promised restoration.

days.reflectionPrompt: What warning, promise, or hope should be heard clearly as Isaiah begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, give me ears to hear Your word with repentance, reverence, and hope.

days.context: Mark is one of the four Gospels, presenting Jesus' identity, teaching, kingdom mission, death, and resurrection. Read this book with attention to its own portrait of Christ, while remembering that every episode serves the larger witness to who Jesus is.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Mark reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.

days.context: Acts follows Luke's Gospel and shows the risen Jesus continuing His mission by the Holy Spirit through His witnesses. The gospel moves from Jerusalem toward the nations through preaching, prayer, suffering, repentance, and Spirit-formed community.

devotional.title: The risen Christ at work

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Acts show the Spirit empowering witness to Jesus?
days.prayerPrompt: Risen Lord, make me faithful by Your Spirit in ordinary witness and love.

days.context: Romans belongs to Paul's apostolic letters, written to churches or coworkers with gospel truth for real belief, worship, holiness, endurance, and shared life. Read commands and encouragements from the foundation of grace in Christ, not as detached religious advice.

devotional.title: Reading Romans as gospel-shaped instruction
devotional.body: Romans is part of Paul's apostolic teaching for churches and believers. Look for how gospel truth leads into worship, identity, holiness, unity, endurance, and love. Keep grace as the root, not merely behavior as the goal.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Romans connect what God has done in Christ with how believers now live?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, let Your grace take root in my belief, worship, relationships, and obedience.

plans.title: New Testament in 1 Year
plans.description: A gentle year-long path through the New Testament with reflection days.
plans.purpose: To let the New Testament settle slowly through repeated reading and reflection.
plans.bestFor: Understanding Jesus, the early church, and Christian living
plans.estimatedTime: 5-10 minutes
plans.coverage: Every New Testament chapter with later reflection readings to help the message sink in.
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Matthew is one of the four Gospels, presenting Jesus' identity, teaching, kingdom mission, death, and resurrection. Read this book with attention to its own portrait of Christ, while remembering that every episode serves the larger witness to who Jesus is.

devotional.title: Following Jesus in Matthew
devotional.body: Matthew presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Matthew reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.

plans.title: Psalms and Proverbs in 1 Year
plans.description: A slow yearly rhythm through prayer, worship, and wisdom.
plans.purpose: To shape prayer and daily wisdom through repeated exposure to Psalms and Proverbs.
plans.bestFor: Decision-making, discernment, and daily wisdom
plans.estimatedTime: 5-10 minutes
plans.coverage: Psalms and Proverbs with reflection readings across the year.
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Psalms stands among Scripture's wisdom and worship books, where prayer, praise, lament, desire, suffering, limits, and practical discernment are brought before God. Read slowly, allowing the genre to shape worship and wisdom before immediate application.

devotional.title: Learning prayer and wisdom in Psalms
devotional.body: Psalms trains the heart as well as the mind. Read for worship, honest prayer, wisdom, limits, longing, and faithful living before God. Let the passage shape what you love, fear, ask, confess, and practice.

days.reflectionPrompt: What desire, prayer, or wisdom is Psalms forming in you today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, shape my heart with wisdom, worship, and honest prayer.

days.context: Proverbs stands among Scripture's wisdom and worship books, where prayer, praise, lament, desire, suffering, limits, and practical discernment are brought before God. Read slowly, allowing the genre to shape worship and wisdom before immediate application.

plans.title: Bible in 30 Days
plans.description: A fast overview pace through the whole Bible.
plans.purpose: To give an intensive, big-picture sweep of Scripture rather than a slow devotional pace.
plans.bestFor: Experienced readers or short focused seasons where overview matters more than detail.
plans.estimatedTime: 45-75 minutes
plans.coverage: A path from Genesis 1-40 through James 5; 1 Peter 1-5; 2 Peter 1-3; 1 John 1-5; 2 John 1; 3 John 1; Jude 1; Revelation 1-22, covering the whole Bible in arranged daily portions.
plans.rhythm: Read for the broad movement of the story, note one major theme, pray briefly, then return later for deeper study.

days.context: Genesis stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Genesis
devotional.body: Genesis belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Genesis begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.

days.context: Exodus stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Exodus
devotional.body: Exodus belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Exodus begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.

days.context: Today's assigned portion first enters Leviticus, Numbers. Pause at each book boundary; the readings have distinct settings and should not be treated as one continuous scene or letter.

devotional.title: Entering Leviticus, Numbers
devotional.body: Leviticus: Leviticus belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application. Numbers: Numbers belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.observationQuestion: Where does each new book begin in today's reading, and what changes in setting, speaker, or genre?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which new book would benefit from a slower rereading?
days.prayer: Lord, help me hear each part of Your word in its own setting.
days.gentleAction: Mark the book transitions in today's reading before moving to application.

days.context: Deuteronomy stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Deuteronomy

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Deuteronomy begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.

days.context: Joshua belongs to the historical books, where Israel's life in the land, leadership, worship, failure, judgment, and mercy unfold in real events. Read this book as part of God's covenant dealings rather than as isolated moral examples.

devotional.title: Entering Joshua
devotional.body: Joshua tells part of Israel's lived history with the Lord. Watch for faithfulness and failure, leadership and worship, judgment and mercy. These chapters are not merely examples to imitate or avoid; they show how God's purposes continue through real people and real consequences.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Joshua show about the Lord's faithfulness in the middle of human faithfulness and failure?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, teach me to read history with humility, repentance, and trust in Your purposes.

plans.title: Bible in 90 Days
plans.description: A strong three-month path through the whole Bible.
plans.purpose: To move through the whole Bible in a focused season while still leaving room to notice repeated themes and book transitions.
plans.bestFor: Readers who want strong momentum and can set aside a meaningful daily reading window.
plans.estimatedTime: About 35–70 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: A path from Genesis 1-14 through Revelation 10-22, covering the whole Bible in arranged daily portions.
plans.rhythm: Read attentively for the passage flow, note one repeated theme, pray, then mark the day complete.

days.context: Genesis stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

plans.title: Bible Overview in 60 Days
plans.description: A two-month overview of the Bible's major movements.
plans.purpose: To help readers see the Bible's main storyline and major movements before choosing books for slower study.
plans.bestFor: Readers wanting orientation to the whole Bible without beginning with a full-year plan.
plans.estimatedTime: 35-60 minutes
plans.coverage: 60 readings beginning with Genesis 1-20 and ending with Revelation 4-22.
plans.rhythm: Read for orientation, notice the book or covenant setting, and write one question for future deeper study.

days.context: Genesis stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Genesis
devotional.body: Genesis belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.context: Isaiah opens by exposing Judah's rebellion, empty worship, social injustice, and the Lord's call to cleansing and repentance. Keep Isaiah's Judah-and-Zion setting in view: holy judgment, failed trust, servant hope, and promised restoration are being proclaimed through Isaiah 1-5.
days.observationQuestion: What sins does the Lord expose, and what return does He invite?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might outward religion need to become repentance, justice, and renewed obedience?
days.prayer: Holy Lord, cleanse what is false in me and teach me to do good before You.
days.gentleAction: Choose one practical act of justice, mercy, or repentance today.

devotional.title: The Holy One calls His people back
devotional.body: Isaiah begins with a wound diagnosis. God's people have religious activity, but their hearts and public life are far from Him. Yet judgment is not the only word: the Holy One calls them to reason together, be cleansed, and learn to do good.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where might outward religion need to become repentance, justice, and renewed obedience?
days.prayerPrompt: Holy Lord, cleanse what is false in me and teach me to do good before You.

days.context: Isaiah sees the Lord's holiness, is cleansed, and is sent into a hard ministry amid judgment and promise. Keep Isaiah's Judah-and-Zion setting in view: holy judgment, failed trust, servant hope, and promised restoration are being proclaimed through Isaiah 6-10.
days.observationQuestion: What does Isaiah see, confess, receive, and hear?
days.reflectionQuestion: How should God's holiness and grace reshape your readiness to obey?
days.prayer: Holy Lord, cleanse my lips and make me willing to go where You send.
days.gentleAction: Pray Isaiah's words, 'Here am I. Send me,' over one faithful step.

devotional.title: Holy, holy, holy
devotional.body: The prophet's calling begins with worship and cleansing. Isaiah is undone before the Holy One, yet grace touches his guilt. These chapters also hold a promised child, Immanuel hope, and warnings against fear-driven alliances.

days.reflectionPrompt: How should God's holiness and grace reshape your readiness to obey?
days.prayerPrompt: Holy Lord, cleanse my lips and make me willing to go where You send.

days.context: Isaiah promises a Spirit-filled ruler from Jesse's line, then turns to songs of salvation and oracles over the nations. Keep Isaiah's Judah-and-Zion setting in view: holy judgment, failed trust, servant hope, and promised restoration are being proclaimed through Isaiah 11-15.
days.observationQuestion: What kind of ruler is promised, and what future peace is described?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need hope in Christ's righteous reign rather than trust in human power?
days.prayer: Righteous King, rule with wisdom, justice, and peace in me and in Your world.
days.gentleAction: Pray for one place where Christ's justice and peace are needed.

devotional.title: The righteous Branch
devotional.body: Judgment over proud nations is real, but it is not the whole horizon. Isaiah sees a righteous King who will rule with justice and bring peace beyond human ability. God's salvation becomes a song because His rule is both holy and hopeful.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need hope in Christ's righteous reign rather than trust in human power?
days.prayerPrompt: Righteous King, rule with wisdom, justice, and peace in me and in Your world.

days.context: Isaiah speaks oracles concerning Moab, Damascus, Cush, and Egypt, showing the Lord's authority over all nations. Keep Isaiah's Judah-and-Zion setting in view: holy judgment, failed trust, servant hope, and promised restoration are being proclaimed through Isaiah 16-19.
days.observationQuestion: What judgments are named, and what surprising hope appears for Egypt?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does God's concern for the nations enlarge your prayers and expectations?
days.prayer: Lord of all nations, humble pride, heal enemies, and draw peoples to worship You.
days.gentleAction: Pray for a nation or people group beyond your own.

devotional.title: Mercy beyond borders
devotional.body: The prophets are not only interested in Israel's private spirituality. The Lord rules over nations, pride, fear, oppression, and false worship. Even Egypt's oracle contains surprising hope that former enemies may know and worship the Lord.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does God's concern for the nations enlarge your prayers and expectations?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord of all nations, humble pride, heal enemies, and draw peoples to worship You.

This is prophetic language addressed to Jerusalem in exile, not a model for how a person may treat a partner. Read the imagery as part of Ezekiel's warning rather than turning it into permission for abuse.
days.observationQuestion: What kinds of false security are exposed in these chapters?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need the Lord's truthful mercy more than shallow reassurance?
days.prayer: Lord, save me from false comfort and bring me back to faithful love for You.
days.gentleAction: Identify one comforting message you need to test against Scripture.

devotional.title: False comfort and covenant grief
devotional.body: False comfort can sound kind while keeping people from repentance. Ezekiel confronts spiritual leaders who heal wounds lightly and a city that has forgotten grace. The imagery is confronting, but its point is covenant grief: the Lord had loved and rescued His people, and they turned from Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need the Lord's truthful mercy more than shallow reassurance?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, save me from false comfort and bring me back to faithful love for You.

days.context: Ezekiel uses parables and history to show Jerusalem's rebellion while holding out the Lord's future promise. Keep Ezekiel's exilic setting in view: visions, signs, judgment, restored presence, and renewed hearts frame the prophetic witness in Ezekiel 17-20.
days.observationQuestion: What does Ezekiel say about responsibility, history, and the Lord's promised future?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need to remember grace honestly without excusing rebellion?
days.prayer: Lord, help me remember Your mercy truthfully and follow You with an undivided heart.
days.gentleAction: List one mercy from your past that should lead to faithfulness today.

devotional.title: Grace remembered, rebellion exposed
devotional.body: The Lord remembers Israel's story more truly than Israel does. He exposes repeated rebellion, but He also promises a tender sprig that He Himself will plant. Responsibility matters, history matters, and grace is still the Lord's work from beginning to end.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to remember grace honestly without excusing rebellion?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, help me remember Your mercy truthfully and follow You with an undivided heart.

days.context: Ezekiel announces judgment, exposes corrupt leadership, and marks Jerusalem's siege with painful prophetic signs. Chapter 23 uses graphic covenant imagery; chapter 24 includes the death of Ezekiel's wife and an unusual instruction concerning public mourning. That sign belongs to this specific prophetic moment and is not a rule against grieving. The imagery gives no permission for abuse.
days.observationQuestion: What people, institutions, and false hopes are judged in these chapters?
days.reflectionQuestion: What security would collapse if it were not anchored in the Lord?
days.prayer: Lord, remove false confidence and anchor me in Your righteous rule.
days.gentleAction: Name one thing you rely on that cannot carry the weight of your hope.

devotional.title: The end of false security
devotional.body: These chapters refuse to let false security survive. Kings, priests, prophets, and people are all weighed by the Lord's holiness. Ezekiel's personal sorrow also shows that judgment is not an abstract idea; sin tears through real lives.

days.reflectionPrompt: What security would collapse if it were not anchored in the Lord?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, remove false confidence and anchor me in Your righteous rule.

days.context: The Lord speaks judgment against surrounding nations, especially Tyre, for pride, violence, and rejoicing over Judah's fall. Keep Ezekiel's exilic setting in view: visions, signs, judgment, restored presence, and renewed hearts frame the prophetic witness in Ezekiel 25-28.
days.observationQuestion: What attitudes and actions are condemned among the surrounding nations?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do pride, success, or comparison quietly shape your sense of security?
days.prayer: King of the nations, humble my pride and teach me to trust Your rule.
days.gentleAction: Turn one boast into thanksgiving before the Lord.

devotional.title: Pride among the nations
devotional.body: Ezekiel widens the view from Jerusalem to the nations. The Lord rules over every people, economy, ruler, and boast. Pride may look secure for a season, but no nation can exalt itself above the God who made the seas and the coastlands.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do pride, success, or comparison quietly shape your sense of security?
days.prayerPrompt: King of the nations, humble my pride and teach me to trust Your rule.

days.context: Ezekiel announces judgment on Egypt and Pharaoh, using images of monsters, trees, and descent to the grave. Keep Ezekiel's exilic setting in view: visions, signs, judgment, restored presence, and renewed hearts frame the prophetic witness in Ezekiel 29-32.
days.observationQuestion: What images does Ezekiel use to describe Egypt's pride and downfall?
days.reflectionQuestion: What impressive power are you tempted to fear or trust more than the Lord?
days.prayer: Lord, You are greater than every power that frightens or fascinates me.
days.gentleAction: Pray for humility in the way you think about earthly power.

devotional.title: Egypt brought low
devotional.body: Egypt represents impressive power that cannot finally save. Pharaoh's boast is answered by the Lord's sovereignty. The passage teaches that political strength, military confidence, and ancient prestige all bow before the One who judges nations justly.

days.reflectionPrompt: What impressive power are you tempted to fear or trust more than the Lord?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, You are greater than every power that frightens or fascinates me.

days.context: Ezekiel is renewed as watchman, Israel's shepherds are judged, and the Lord promises cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit. Keep Ezekiel's exilic setting in view: visions, signs, judgment, restored presence, and renewed hearts frame the prophetic witness in Ezekiel 33-36.
days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord promise to do for His people in these chapters?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need more than self-improvement: a heart renewed by God?
days.prayer: Lord, cleanse me, give me a tender heart, and lead me as my true Shepherd.
days.gentleAction: Pray Ezekiel 36:26 in your own words.

devotional.title: Watchman, shepherd, new heart
devotional.body: After judgment, restoration begins with the Lord's own name and mercy. Bad shepherds are confronted, scattered sheep are sought, and hard hearts are promised renewal. Hope rests not in Israel improving itself, but in the Lord giving His people a new heart and Spirit.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need more than self-improvement: a heart renewed by God?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, cleanse me, give me a tender heart, and lead me as my true Shepherd.

days.context: The exiles say their hope is lost. In Ezekiel 37:11 the Lord identifies the dry bones as the whole house of Israel, then promises to restore His people by His word and Spirit. The following chapters speak of reunion under one shepherd, conflict, and a vision of restored worship. Begin with Israel's exilic setting before making a Christian or personal application.
days.observationQuestion: Who does the Lord say the bones represent in verse 11, and what does He promise in verses 12-14?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need hope that depends on God's Spirit rather than your strength?
days.prayer: Faithful Lord, thank You for speaking hope to Your exiled people. Help me trust Your word and Spirit without turning Your promise into a prediction about my circumstances.
days.gentleAction: Read Ezekiel 37:11-14 again, name God's promise to Israel, and bring one present concern to Him without prescribing its outcome.

devotional.title: Dry bones and returning hope
devotional.body: The dry bones first portray Israel's lost hope in exile. God promises to restore His people, put His Spirit in them, and bring them home. The vision shows that restoration depends on His word and Spirit, not human strength. Christians may hear an echo of resurrection hope, but the passage does not promise that every private situation will turn out as we wish.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need hope that depends on God's Spirit rather than your strength?
days.prayerPrompt: Faithful Lord, thank You for speaking hope to Your exiled people. Help me trust Your word and Spirit without turning Your promise into a prediction about my circumstances.

days.context: Ezekiel continues the temple vision, sees the Lord's glory return, and hears instructions about holiness and worship. Keep Ezekiel's exilic setting in view: visions, signs, judgment, restored presence, and renewed hearts frame the prophetic witness in Ezekiel 41-44.
days.observationQuestion: What details emphasize holiness, order, and the return of the Lord's glory?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might reverence for God's presence reshape ordinary parts of your life?
days.prayer: Lord, make my life a place of reverent attention to Your holy presence.
days.gentleAction: Choose one ordinary space or routine to dedicate consciously to the Lord.

devotional.title: A holy dwelling
devotional.body: The measurements can feel slow, but they teach order, holiness, and reverence. Restoration is not merely getting land back; it is the return of the Lord's glory. His people are called to live around His presence with renewed awe.

days.reflectionPrompt: How might reverence for God's presence reshape ordinary parts of your life?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, make my life a place of reverent attention to Your holy presence.

days.context: Ezekiel's vision concludes with restored worship, renewed land, a life-giving river, and a city named for the Lord's presence. Keep Ezekiel's exilic setting in view: visions, signs, judgment, restored presence, and renewed hearts frame the prophetic witness in Ezekiel 45-48.
days.observationQuestion: What signs of restored worship, justice, life, and presence appear in these chapters?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you long to know, in a settled way, that the Lord is there?
days.prayer: Lord, let Your presence be my hope, my home, and my life.
days.gentleAction: Write the phrase 'The Lord is there' beside one concern you are carrying.

devotional.title: The Lord is there
devotional.body: Ezekiel ends not with exile but with presence. The river flowing from the temple brings life wherever it goes, and the final name of the city is the deepest promise: the Lord is there. Restoration is finally about dwelling with Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you long to know, in a settled way, that the Lord is there?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, let Your presence be my hope, my home, and my life.

days.context: Daniel and his friends serve in Babylon while remaining faithful, interpreting dreams, facing the furnace, and seeing a proud king humbled. These opening chapters move from food-table faithfulness to imperial dreams and the fiery furnace, showing that the God of Israel gives wisdom and humbles Babylonian pride.
days.observationQuestion: How do Daniel and his friends remain faithful, and how does the Lord act?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need quiet courage to remain faithful in a pressured environment?
days.prayer: Lord, give me wisdom, courage, and humility wherever You have placed me.
days.gentleAction: Choose one small act of faithfulness you can practice without needing attention.

devotional.title: Faithful in exile
devotional.body: Daniel shows faithfulness under pressure without pretending exile is easy. The Lord gives wisdom, preserves His servants, and humbles kings. Even in Babylon, no ruler has the final word over those who belong to God.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need quiet courage to remain faithful in a pressured environment?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, give me wisdom, courage, and humility wherever You have placed me.

days.context: Daniel interprets Babylon's fall, survives the lions' den, and receives visions of kingdoms that rise and pass away. The handwriting, lions' den, and beastly visions together teach that arrogant empires are weighed by God and that the Ancient of Days rules beyond their violence.
days.observationQuestion: What do these chapters reveal about rulers, kingdoms, prayer, and God's authority?
days.reflectionQuestion: What current fear becomes smaller when you remember that earthly kingdoms pass away?
days.prayer: Ancient of Days, steady my heart under Your everlasting rule.
days.gentleAction: Pray for Daniel-like faithfulness in one pressure you face today.

devotional.title: Kingdoms weighed and passing
devotional.body: Earthly kingdoms can look overwhelming, but Daniel insists they are accountable to God. Proud rulers are weighed, faithful prayer is tested, and beastly powers do not last forever. The Ancient of Days reigns when history looks unstable.

days.reflectionPrompt: What current fear becomes smaller when you remember that earthly kingdoms pass away?
days.prayerPrompt: Ancient of Days, steady my heart under Your everlasting rule.

days.context: Daniel prays confession over Israel's exile and receives visions of conflict, endurance, and final resurrection hope. The final chapters join penitential prayer with difficult apocalyptic hope, calling God's people to wisdom and endurance until the promised resurrection.
days.observationQuestion: How does Daniel pray, and what hope is given to God's people in the final chapters?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need endurance that is rooted in confession, mercy, and resurrection hope?
days.prayer: Lord, have mercy, give endurance, and keep my hope fixed on Your final victory.
days.gentleAction: Pray a short confession, then thank the Lord for hope beyond what you can see.

devotional.title: Hope beyond exile
devotional.body: Daniel's hope is deeply prayerful. He does not treat prophecy as curiosity, but responds with confession, humility, and trust. The final visions are difficult, yet they lift the reader toward endurance and resurrection: the Lord has not lost control of history.

days.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need endurance that is rooted in confession, mercy, and resurrection hope?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, have mercy, give endurance, and keep my hope fixed on Your final victory.

plans.title: Acts and the Early Church
plans.description: Follow the birth and spread of the early church through Acts.
plans.purpose: To move steadily through Jesus' life, the early church, and the letters.
plans.bestFor: Understanding Jesus, the early church, and Christian living
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: 28 readings beginning with Acts 1 and ending with Acts 28.
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: The risen Jesus teaches His apostles, promises the Holy Spirit, ascends, and prepares them for witness. The opening chapter bridges Luke's Gospel and Acts, making clear that the mission waits for promised power from the Spirit rather than beginning in apostolic enthusiasm.
days.observationQuestion: What does Jesus promise, and what mission does He give His witnesses?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need to wait on the Lord rather than rush ahead in your own strength?
days.prayer: Risen Lord, make me a faithful witness by the power of Your Spirit.
days.gentleAction: Pray for one ordinary opportunity to bear witness to Christ today.

devotional.title: Witnesses by the Spirit
