days.context: Isaiah belongs to the prophetic witness, where the Lord addresses covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, idolatry, judgment, mercy, and future hope. Read the opening section as God's word to His people before turning it into private prediction or general advice.

devotional.title: Listening to Isaiah
devotional.body: Isaiah speaks into covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, judgment, mercy, and hope. Prophetic books are not mainly prediction puzzles; they call God's people to hear His word, return to Him, and trust His promised restoration.

plans.title: New Testament Overview
plans.description: A broad chapter-by-chapter overview of the New Testament.
plans.purpose: To help readers see the New Testament's flow from Jesus' ministry to the church's witness, apostolic teaching, and final hope.
plans.bestFor: Readers who want a broad New Testament orientation before slower study.
plans.estimatedTime: 20-35 minutes
plans.coverage: 30 readings beginning with Matthew 1-9 and ending with Revelation 15-22.
plans.rhythm: Read for how each section bears witness to Christ, forms His people, and calls for faithful response.

days.context: Matthew is one of the four Gospels, presenting Jesus' identity, teaching, kingdom mission, death, and resurrection. Read this book with attention to its own portrait of Christ, while remembering that every episode serves the larger witness to who Jesus is.

devotional.title: Following Jesus in Matthew
devotional.body: Matthew presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Matthew reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Romans connect what God has done in Christ with how believers now live?

plans.title: Bible Story in 30 Days
plans.description: Follow creation, covenant, Jesus, the church and new creation through selected chapters.
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: 30 selected chapters, not every chapter of the Bible.
plans.purpose: To give a manageable overview before choosing where to study more deeply.
plans.bestFor: Seeing the big picture before deeper study
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Genesis stands within the Torah, the opening five-book foundation of Scripture. These books establish creation, promise, covenant, rescue from bondage, worship, holiness, and life before the Lord. Read the opening section as foundation for the Bible's larger story.

devotional.title: Beginning Genesis
devotional.body: Genesis belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Genesis begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.
days.observationQuestion: What do you notice in Genesis 1 about the people, setting, and the Lord's action?

days.context: Genesis 3 follows the good creation and human vocation of Genesis 1-2. The serpent disputes God's word; the man and woman disobey, hide, and blame. Read the chapter's judgments and God's care for them together.

devotional.title: Trust broken in the garden
devotional.body: The story names a rupture with God, with one another, and with the ground. God questions the pair and announces consequences; He also clothes them before they leave the garden. Do not skip either human responsibility or God's continued care.

days.observationQuestion: How do the serpent, woman, and man each speak about God's command, and what changes after they eat?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where does this chapter help you name mistrust or blame truthfully rather than hide it?
days.prayer: Lord, help me hear Your word, own my wrongdoing, and seek Your mercy.

days.context: After the scattering at Babel, the Lord calls Abram to leave his country and promises land, descendants, and blessing that will reach all families of the earth.

devotional.title: Abram is called
devotional.body: The story begins with God's initiative and Abram's journey. Read the promise to Abram in its own setting before tracing how later Scripture understands blessing for the nations.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord command Abram, what does He promise, and how does Abram respond?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might God's purpose to bless others shape the way you read the rest of this story?
days.prayer: Lord, help me hear Your call and trust Your faithful purposes.

days.context: Abram worries because he remains childless. The Lord answers with a promise about descendants, and the chapter closes with a covenant concerning land and a future that includes hardship.

devotional.title: Promise amid waiting
devotional.body: Abram believes the Lord, and the Lord counts it to him as righteousness. The promise does not mean the wait or coming suffering vanishes. Keep God's specific covenant with Abram distinct from a guarantee about every reader's wishes.

days.observationQuestion: What concern does Abram bring, and what does the Lord promise in verses 1-6 and 13-18?
days.reflectionQuestion: What do Abram's honest questions teach you about bringing uncertainty before God?
days.prayer: Faithful Lord, teach me to trust You without demanding that my waiting follow Abram's story.

days.context: Genesis 22 describes a specific test of Abraham after the promised birth of Isaac. The messenger stops Abraham, forbids harm to the boy, and a ram is provided in his place.

devotional.title: The Lord provides
devotional.body: This disturbing account must not be turned into a pattern for harming a child or obeying a private impression to do so. Attend to God's interruption, the provision, and the renewed promise to Abraham before drawing later Christian connections.

days.observationQuestion: Who stops Abraham in verses 11-12, what is provided, and what promise follows?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the text's refusal of Isaac's death shape your reading of the test?
days.prayer: Lord, keep me attentive to Your word and protective of those entrusted to my care.

days.context: This plan samples Exodus 3, its first reading from Exodus, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Exodus's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Exodus: Exodus 3
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Exodus's larger argument or story. Exodus belongs to the Torah, where Scripture lays foundations for creation, covenant, rescue, holiness, wilderness faith, and life with the Lord. Read this section slowly, asking how God's character and covenant purposes are being revealed before rushing to application.

days.reflectionPrompt: What foundation for knowing the Lord is being laid as Exodus begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, ground my faith in Your character, Your promises, and Your covenant mercy.
days.observationQuestion: What does Exodus 3 reveal within Exodus, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: The Lord gives Israel instructions for the Passover while they are still in Egypt. Households mark their doors, share a meal, and prepare to leave; the chapter also records judgment and the beginning of the exodus.

devotional.title: Passover and deliverance
devotional.body: Passover belongs first to Israel's rescue from slavery and its remembered worship. Its details are not instructions for Christians to imitate the doorpost ritual. Read the commanded remembrance and costly deliverance before tracing later connections to Christ.

days.observationQuestion: What are Israelite households told to do, and how is this night to be remembered?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does this account show about rescue and remembrance without making it a promise of exemption from all danger?
days.prayer: Lord, help me remember Your saving acts with reverence and gratitude.

days.context: Israel has been rescued from Egypt before the commandments are spoken at Sinai. The chapter begins by naming the Lord as their deliverer, then addresses worship, family, speech, rest, and neighbourly conduct.

devotional.title: A covenant people learn to live
devotional.body: The commandments form covenant life for a redeemed people; they are not a ladder by which Israel first earns rescue. Notice both devotion to God and responsibility toward neighbours as you read.

days.observationQuestion: How does the Lord introduce Himself in verses 1-2, and which commands address life with neighbours?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where would truthful worship change the way you treat another person?
days.prayer: Delivering Lord, teach me to honour You and love my neighbours faithfully.

days.context: Moses addresses Israel as they prepare to enter the land. Deuteronomy 6 calls them to hear that the Lord is one, love Him wholeheartedly, teach His words to their children, and remember His rescue from Egypt.

devotional.title: Love the Lord and remember
devotional.body: This selected chapter is not the beginning of Deuteronomy. Its call to love the Lord belongs to Israel's covenant life, including remembered deliverance and daily teaching. Read the command with its audience and story before applying its wisdom to your own worship and household.

days.observationQuestion: Who is addressed in verses 3-7, and what rescue are they told to remember in verses 20-25?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might remembering God's prior faithfulness shape what you teach or practice today?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to love You with my whole life and to remember Your faithfulness.

days.context: This plan samples Joshua 24, its first reading from Joshua, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Joshua's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Joshua: Joshua 24
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Joshua's larger argument or story. Joshua tells part of Israel's lived history with the Lord. Watch for faithfulness and failure, leadership and worship, judgment and mercy. These chapters are not merely examples to imitate or avoid; they show how God's purposes continue through real people and real consequences.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Joshua show about the Lord's faithfulness in the middle of human faithfulness and failure?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, teach me to read history with humility, repentance, and trust in Your purposes.
days.observationQuestion: What does Joshua 24 reveal within Joshua, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: Ruth belongs to the historical books, where Israel's life in the land, leadership, worship, failure, judgment, and mercy unfold in real events. Read this book as part of God's covenant dealings rather than as isolated moral examples.

devotional.title: Entering Ruth
devotional.body: Ruth tells part of Israel's lived history with the Lord. Watch for faithfulness and failure, leadership and worship, judgment and mercy. These chapters are not merely examples to imitate or avoid; they show how God's purposes continue through real people and real consequences.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Ruth show about the Lord's faithfulness in the middle of human faithfulness and failure?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, teach me to read history with humility, repentance, and trust in Your purposes.
days.observationQuestion: What do you notice in Ruth 1 about the people, setting, and the Lord's action?

devotional.title: First stop in 2 Samuel: 2 Samuel 7
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of 2 Samuel's larger argument or story. 2 Samuel tells part of Israel's lived history with the Lord. Watch for faithfulness and failure, leadership and worship, judgment and mercy. These chapters are not merely examples to imitate or avoid; they show how God's purposes continue through real people and real consequences.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does 2 Samuel show about the Lord's faithfulness in the middle of human faithfulness and failure?

days.context: This plan samples Psalm 23, its first reading from Psalms, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Psalms's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Psalms: Psalm 23
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Psalms's larger argument or story. Psalms trains the heart as well as the mind. Read for worship, honest prayer, wisdom, limits, longing, and faithful living before God. Let the passage shape what you love, fear, ask, confess, and practice.

days.reflectionPrompt: What desire, prayer, or wisdom is Psalms forming in you today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, shape my heart with wisdom, worship, and honest prayer.
days.observationQuestion: What does Psalm 23 reveal within Psalms, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: This plan samples Isaiah 9, its first reading from Isaiah, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Isaiah's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Isaiah: Isaiah 9
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Isaiah's larger argument or story. Isaiah speaks into covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, judgment, mercy, and hope. Prophetic books are not mainly prediction puzzles; they call God's people to hear His word, return to Him, and trust His promised restoration.

days.reflectionPrompt: What warning, promise, or hope should be heard clearly as Isaiah begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, give me ears to hear Your word with repentance, reverence, and hope.
days.observationQuestion: What does Isaiah 9 reveal within Isaiah, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: Isaiah's Servant is rejected, bears others' iniquities, and is later vindicated. Read the chapter with the surrounding Servant passage in Isaiah 52:13-53:12 in view.

devotional.title: The suffering Servant
devotional.body: The poem links the Servant's suffering with the wrongdoing of others rather than celebrating suffering for its own sake. Christians read it in light of Jesus' death and resurrection (see Acts 8:32-35); that connection should be explained, not assumed or used to excuse harm.

days.observationQuestion: What does the passage say the Servant suffers, for whom, and what follows his suffering?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the Servant's bearing of others' wrongdoing invite gratitude without asking the harmed to remain unsafe?
days.prayer: Lord, help me read the Servant's suffering with humility and hope.

devotional.title: First stop in Jeremiah: Jeremiah 31
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Jeremiah's larger argument or story. Jeremiah speaks into covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, judgment, mercy, and hope. Prophetic books are not mainly prediction puzzles; they call God's people to hear His word, return to Him, and trust His promised restoration.

days.reflectionPrompt: What warning, promise, or hope should be heard clearly as Jeremiah begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, give me ears to hear Your word with repentance, reverence, and hope.
days.observationQuestion: What does Jeremiah 31 reveal within Jeremiah, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

devotional.title: First stop in Ezekiel: Ezekiel 36
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Ezekiel's larger argument or story. Ezekiel speaks into covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, judgment, mercy, and hope. Prophetic books are not mainly prediction puzzles; they call God's people to hear His word, return to Him, and trust His promised restoration.

days.reflectionPrompt: What warning, promise, or hope should be heard clearly as Ezekiel begins?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, give me ears to hear Your word with repentance, reverence, and hope.
days.observationQuestion: What does Ezekiel 36 reveal within Ezekiel, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: Luke is one of the four Gospels, presenting Jesus' identity, teaching, kingdom mission, death, and resurrection. Read this book with attention to its own portrait of Christ, while remembering that every episode serves the larger witness to who Jesus is.

devotional.title: Following Jesus in Luke
devotional.body: Luke presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Luke reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.
days.observationQuestion: What do you notice in Luke 1 about the people, setting, and the Lord's action?

days.context: Luke sets Jesus' birth under an imperial census and places Mary and Joseph in Bethlehem. Shepherds hear the angelic announcement; later, Simeon and Anna speak over the child in the temple.

devotional.title: The Savior is born
devotional.body: Luke holds humble circumstances alongside the announcement of a Savior. The shepherds' witness and the temple voices connect this child's arrival to Israel's hope; do not reduce the chapter to a peaceful scene without its wider promises.

days.observationQuestion: Who hears about Jesus, what titles or hopes are spoken, and how do they respond?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does Luke's choice of witnesses draw your attention to about Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me receive the news of Your coming with wonder and faith.

days.context: This plan samples Matthew 5, its first reading from Matthew, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Matthew's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Matthew: Matthew 5
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Matthew's larger argument or story. Matthew presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Matthew reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.
days.observationQuestion: What does Matthew 5 reveal within Matthew, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: This plan samples Mark 4, its first reading from Mark, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Mark's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Mark: Mark 4
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Mark's larger argument or story. Mark presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Mark reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.
days.observationQuestion: What does Mark 4 reveal within Mark, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: Jesus speaks these parables while tax collectors and sinners draw near and religious critics object to His welcome. Read the lost sheep, lost coin, and two sons within that conversation.

devotional.title: Joy over the lost
devotional.body: Each story presses the joy of finding what was lost. The final parable also leaves the elder son's response open, turning the critics' complaint back on them. Notice the father's welcome without flattening the younger son's wrongdoing or the elder son's resentment.

days.observationQuestion: What prompts Jesus to tell these stories, and who rejoices or refuses to join the joy?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might you need to receive mercy or welcome another's return?
days.prayer: Merciful Father, help me rejoice in Your grace without hiding my need for it.

days.context: This plan samples John 11, its first reading from John, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within John's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in John: John 11
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of John's larger argument or story. John presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does John reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.
days.observationQuestion: What does John 11 reveal within John, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: John 19 follows Jesus' arrest and trial. Notice the royal language, the people present at the cross, Jesus' words before death, and the care taken in His burial.

devotional.title: The crucified King
devotional.body: John presents Jesus' real suffering and death without turning the cross into a mere example of courage. His final cry belongs in the scene of His completed work; the burial confirms that He truly died. Read this chapter before moving to the resurrection witnesses in John 20.

days.observationQuestion: What words and actions frame Jesus as King, and what does John report about His death and burial?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does staying with the whole crucifixion account affect your response to Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me face Your cross with gratitude, reverence, and honesty.

days.context: John 20 moves from the empty tomb to Mary's encounter, Jesus' appearance to the gathered disciples, and Thomas' confession. John states his purpose in verses 30-31.

devotional.title: Witnesses to the risen Jesus
devotional.body: The witnesses do not all begin with instant understanding. Mary, the disciples, and Thomas encounter the risen Jesus in distinct scenes. John's stated aim is that readers believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name.

days.observationQuestion: What does each witness see or hear, and what purpose does John give for recording these signs?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which witness's movement toward belief would you like to read more slowly?
days.prayer: Risen Lord Jesus, lead me from hearing the witnesses to trusting You.

days.context: At Pentecost the Spirit enables witness; Peter explains the event by speaking of Jesus' death, resurrection, and exaltation. The crowd asks how to respond, and the chapter ends with the shared life of the new believers.

devotional.title: The Spirit and the first believers
devotional.body: Acts 2 links the Spirit's gift to testimony about the risen Jesus, a call to repent and be baptized, and a community devoted to teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer. Observe these parts together rather than reducing the chapter to a single dramatic moment.

days.observationQuestion: What does Peter say God has done with Jesus, how do hearers respond, and what practices mark the new community?
days.reflectionQuestion: What part of the church's shared life in verses 42-47 invites a concrete step of participation?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, make me attentive to Your Spirit, Your gospel, and the life of Your people.

days.context: Cornelius and Peter each receive a vision. Peter comes to a Gentile household, proclaims Jesus' life, death, and resurrection, and sees the Spirit given while he is speaking.

devotional.title: The gospel reaches Cornelius
devotional.body: Peter learns that he must not treat these Gentile hearers as unclean or exclude them from hearing the gospel. The Spirit's gift surprises Jewish believers who came with him. Follow Peter's message about Jesus as well as the crossing of a social boundary.

days.observationQuestion: What does Peter say about Jesus in verses 34-43, and what surprises those with him in verses 44-48?
days.reflectionQuestion: Who might you wrongly assume is beyond hearing the good news?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, keep me from favouritism and make me ready to share Your good news.

days.context: This plan samples Romans 3, its first reading from Romans, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Romans's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Romans: Romans 3
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Romans's larger argument or story. Romans is part of Paul's apostolic teaching for churches and believers. Look for how gospel truth leads into worship, identity, holiness, unity, endurance, and love. Keep grace as the root, not merely behavior as the goal.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Romans connect what God has done in Christ with how believers now live?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, let Your grace take root in my belief, worship, relationships, and obedience.
days.observationQuestion: What does Romans 3 reveal within Romans, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: This plan samples Ephesians 2, its first reading from Ephesians, rather than necessarily starting at chapter 1. Read the chapter within Ephesians's larger setting before drawing a conclusion from this selection.

devotional.title: First stop in Ephesians: Ephesians 2
devotional.body: This selected chapter is one part of Ephesians's larger argument or story. Ephesians is part of Paul's apostolic teaching for churches and believers. Look for how gospel truth leads into worship, identity, holiness, unity, endurance, and love. Keep grace as the root, not merely behavior as the goal.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Ephesians connect what God has done in Christ with how believers now live?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, let Your grace take root in my belief, worship, relationships, and obedience.
days.observationQuestion: What does Ephesians 2 reveal within Ephesians, and what would you need to read around it for more context?

days.context: John's vision follows the judgment scenes of Revelation 20. Chapter 21 pictures a new heaven and earth, the holy city, God's dwelling with His people, and the removal of death and tears.

devotional.title: God dwells with His people
devotional.body: This is a vision of God's future renewal, not a promise that present grief has already ended. Its centre is God's presence with His people. Hold the hope of verses 1-5 alongside the chapter's call to faithful endurance rather than using it to rush another person's sorrow.

days.observationQuestion: What does John see in verses 1-5, and what does the voice say God will do?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can future hope make room for honest grief and faithful living now?
days.prayer: God of hope, keep me near You in present sorrow as I await Your promised renewal.

plans.title: Bible Story in 60 Days
plans.description: A more spacious introduction to Scripture's story through 60 selected chapters.
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: 60 selected chapters, not every chapter of the Bible.
plans.purpose: To give a manageable overview before choosing where to study more deeply.
plans.bestFor: Seeing the big picture before deeper study
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Genesis opens with God speaking, ordering, and blessing creation. Humanity, male and female, is made in God's image and given a vocation within the world He calls good.

devotional.title: God creates and blesses
devotional.body: The chapter begins with God's initiative, not human achievement. Its repeated goodness grounds human dignity and responsibility; it does not answer every modern question about the mechanics of creation.

days.observationQuestion: What does God make, bless, and call good, and what task is given to humanity?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might shared image-bearing dignity change the way you regard another person?
days.prayer: Creator God, teach me to receive Your world with gratitude and care.

days.context: Genesis 2 draws close to the human scene: the Lord forms the man, plants a garden, gives work and a boundary, and makes a fitting partner. The chapter ends with union and openness.

devotional.title: Life in the garden
devotional.body: Read this alongside Genesis 1 rather than treating the two chapters as competing stories. The human vocation includes cultivation and care; the boundary reminds the reader that freedom is lived before God.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord give the humans, and what limit does He set?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where does receiving life as gift change your sense of work or relationship?
days.prayer: Lord, help me tend what You entrust to me with gratitude.

days.context: Genesis 3 follows the good creation and human vocation of Genesis 1-2. The serpent disputes God's word; the man and woman disobey, hide, and blame. Read the chapter's judgments and God's care for them together.

devotional.title: Trust broken in the garden
devotional.body: The story names a rupture with God, with one another, and with the ground. God questions the pair and announces consequences; He also clothes them before they leave the garden. Do not skip either human responsibility or God's continued care.

days.observationQuestion: How do the serpent, woman, and man each speak about God's command, and what changes after they eat?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where does this chapter help you name mistrust or blame truthfully rather than hide it?
days.prayer: Lord, help me hear Your word, own my wrongdoing, and seek Your mercy.

days.context: After the flood, God blesses Noah's family and makes a covenant with them and every living creature. The chapter also records Noah's failure and its effect on his family.

devotional.title: A covenant after the flood
devotional.body: The rainbow marks God's promise not to destroy all flesh by flood again. This is a covenant with living creatures, not a guarantee that no local flood or human evil will occur. Hold the promise and the chapter's sober ending together.

days.observationQuestion: Who receives the covenant in verses 8-17, and what exactly is promised?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does God's care for living creatures affect the way you receive this promise?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You for Your patience with a wounded world.

days.context: After the scattering at Babel, the Lord calls Abram to leave his country and promises land, descendants, and blessing that will reach all families of the earth.

devotional.title: Abram is called
devotional.body: The story begins with God's initiative and Abram's journey. Read the promise to Abram in its own setting before tracing how later Scripture understands blessing for the nations.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord command Abram, what does He promise, and how does Abram respond?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might God's purpose to bless others shape the way you read the rest of this story?
days.prayer: Lord, help me hear Your call and trust Your faithful purposes.

days.context: Returning from Egypt, Abram and Lot have too many flocks for the land to support them together. Abram offers Lot a choice; afterward the Lord repeats His promise to Abram.

devotional.title: Abram and Lot separate
devotional.body: Lot chooses a fertile-looking region near Sodom, while Abram receives God's specific land promise. Do not turn the contrast into a rule that generosity always brings property or wealth.

days.observationQuestion: What causes the dispute, who chooses first, and what does the Lord promise Abram afterward?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could generosity help resolve a real conflict without trying to control its outcome?
days.prayer: Lord, make me peaceable and attentive to Your promises.

days.context: Abram worries because he remains childless. The Lord answers with a promise about descendants, and the chapter closes with a covenant concerning land and a future that includes hardship.

devotional.title: Promise amid waiting
devotional.body: Abram believes the Lord, and the Lord counts it to him as righteousness. The promise does not mean the wait or coming suffering vanishes. Keep God's specific covenant with Abram distinct from a guarantee about every reader's wishes.

days.observationQuestion: What concern does Abram bring, and what does the Lord promise in verses 1-6 and 13-18?
days.reflectionQuestion: What do Abram's honest questions teach you about bringing uncertainty before God?
days.prayer: Faithful Lord, teach me to trust You without demanding that my waiting follow Abram's story.

days.context: The Lord reaffirms His covenant with Abram, changes Abram's and Sarai's names, appoints circumcision as its sign, and promises a son through Sarah.

devotional.title: The covenant marked in a family
devotional.body: The promise is given to this family within a long wait; it is not a guarantee of a child for every reader. Notice Sarah's named place in the promise and the difference between God's word about Isaac and Abraham's concern for Ishmael.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord promise, what sign is commanded, and how are Sarah and Ishmael addressed?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does this chapter hold promise and long waiting together?
days.prayer: Faithful Lord, help me honour Your promises without claiming another family's story as my own.

days.context: Genesis 22 describes a specific test of Abraham after the promised birth of Isaac. The messenger stops Abraham, forbids harm to the boy, and a ram is provided in his place.

devotional.title: The Lord provides
devotional.body: This disturbing account must not be turned into a pattern for harming a child or obeying a private impression to do so. Attend to God's interruption, the provision, and the renewed promise to Abraham before drawing later Christian connections.

days.observationQuestion: Who stops Abraham in verses 11-12, what is provided, and what promise follows?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the text's refusal of Isaac's death shape your reading of the test?
days.prayer: Lord, keep me attentive to Your word and protective of those entrusted to my care.

days.context: After years of separation and hardship, Joseph tells his brothers who he is. He names their sale of him into Egypt and describes how God has preserved life through the famine.

devotional.title: Joseph reveals himself
devotional.body: Joseph's account of providence does not make his brothers' betrayal good or require every harmed person to reconcile quickly. Observe his tears, their fear, and the practical provision for the family.

days.observationQuestion: What wrong does Joseph name, what purpose does he see, and how does he provide for his family?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can hope for good avoid denying a real wrong?
days.prayer: Lord, help me tell the truth about harm and notice Your care.

days.context: While Moses tends a flock, the Lord speaks from the burning bush. He names the suffering of Israel in Egypt, recalls the ancestors' covenant, and sends Moses to Pharaoh.

devotional.title: The Lord sees and sends
devotional.body: God's holy presence begins this rescue, and Moses' objections remain part of the conversation. The divine name is given in the setting of covenant faithfulness, not as a technique for mastering God.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord say He has seen and heard, and how does Moses respond to being sent?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could attending to another person's suffering change the way you pray or act?
days.prayer: Holy Lord, help me listen to Your word and care for those who suffer.

days.context: After Pharaoh increases Israel's burden, the Lord repeats His promise to bring them out, take them as His people, and bring them to the promised land. A genealogy then locates Moses and Aaron within Israel.

devotional.title: A promise to a discouraged people
devotional.body: The people cannot listen because of broken spirit and hard labour. Their exhaustion is not presented as a moral failure. God's covenant words precede the visible change in their circumstances.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord say He will do, and why do the people struggle to hear Moses?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you speak hope without dismissing someone's exhaustion?
days.prayer: Lord, remember those worn down by labour and keep Your word before them.

days.context: The Lord gives Israel instructions for the Passover while they are still in Egypt. Households mark their doors, share a meal, and prepare to leave; the chapter also records judgment and the beginning of the exodus.

devotional.title: Passover and deliverance
devotional.body: Passover belongs first to Israel's rescue from slavery and its remembered worship. Its details are not instructions for Christians to imitate the doorpost ritual. Read the commanded remembrance and costly deliverance before tracing later connections to Christ.

days.observationQuestion: What are Israelite households told to do, and how is this night to be remembered?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does this account show about rescue and remembrance without making it a promise of exemption from all danger?
days.prayer: Lord, help me remember Your saving acts with reverence and gratitude.

days.context: With Pharaoh's army approaching, Israel fears for its life. The Lord tells Moses to lead them forward, divides the sea, and brings the people through while the pursuing force is overwhelmed.

devotional.title: A way through the sea
devotional.body: This is Israel's particular deliverance from slavery and pursuit, not a guarantee that every danger ends in escape. Read the people's fear, the Lord's action, and the costly judgment together.

days.observationQuestion: How do the people and Moses speak at the sea, and what does the Lord do?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can this story lead to gratitude for rescue without making light of current danger?
days.prayer: Delivering Lord, hear those in danger and teach me reverent trust.

days.context: Israel has been rescued from Egypt before the commandments are spoken at Sinai. The chapter begins by naming the Lord as their deliverer, then addresses worship, family, speech, rest, and neighbourly conduct.

devotional.title: A covenant people learn to live
devotional.body: The commandments form covenant life for a redeemed people; they are not a ladder by which Israel first earns rescue. Notice both devotion to God and responsibility toward neighbours as you read.

days.observationQuestion: How does the Lord introduce Himself in verses 1-2, and which commands address life with neighbours?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where would truthful worship change the way you treat another person?
days.prayer: Delivering Lord, teach me to honour You and love my neighbours faithfully.

days.context: Exodus 34 follows Israel's golden calf and Moses' intercession. The Lord renews the covenant and reveals His character while warning Israel against idolatry.

devotional.title: Mercy after the broken covenant
devotional.body: God's mercy does not call the calf harmless, and His justice does not erase His compassion. Read His self-description in verses 6-7 alongside the covenant renewal rather than lifting one phrase out of the story.

days.observationQuestion: How does the Lord describe Himself, and what commands accompany the renewed covenant?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need to receive both God's mercy and His call to faithfulness?
days.prayer: Merciful Lord, keep me from treating Your patience lightly.

days.context: Moses addresses Israel as they prepare to enter the land. Deuteronomy 6 calls them to hear that the Lord is one, love Him wholeheartedly, teach His words to their children, and remember His rescue from Egypt.

devotional.title: Love the Lord and remember
devotional.body: This selected chapter is not the beginning of Deuteronomy. Its call to love the Lord belongs to Israel's covenant life, including remembered deliverance and daily teaching. Read the command with its audience and story before applying its wisdom to your own worship and household.

days.observationQuestion: Who is addressed in verses 3-7, and what rescue are they told to remember in verses 20-25?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might remembering God's prior faithfulness shape what you teach or practice today?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to love You with my whole life and to remember Your faithfulness.

days.context: Moses speaks to Israel near the end of the covenant address. After naming blessing, curse, and possible exile, he speaks of return, God's compassion, and the choice set before the people.

devotional.title: A call to return and choose life
devotional.body: The promised gathering and land belong first to Israel's covenant history; they are not an individual guarantee of prosperity. Notice that God's work on the heart in verse 6 accompanies the call to love and obey Him.

days.observationQuestion: What future does Moses describe in verses 1-10, and what choice does he set before Israel in verses 15-20?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does remembering God's compassion affect your response to His call?
days.prayer: Lord, turn my heart toward love and faithful obedience.

days.context: Joshua gathers Israel at Shechem, recounts the Lord's acts from Abraham through the land, and calls the people to put away other gods and serve the Lord.

devotional.title: Remember and choose whom to serve
devotional.body: The call to choose follows God's prior gift and rescue. Joshua also warns that covenant loyalty is serious; his words are addressed to Israel in its land, not a simple slogan detached from its history.

days.observationQuestion: Which acts of God does Joshua recount before asking the people to choose?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does remembering prior mercy add to a decision about faithfulness?
days.prayer: Lord, keep my worship rooted in gratitude and truth.

days.context: After Joshua's generation dies, Israel turns to other gods. The chapter introduces a recurring pattern: oppression, judges raised up by the Lord, temporary rescue, and renewed unfaithfulness.

devotional.title: A generation forgets
devotional.body: This is a summary of Israel's troubled life in the land, not a formula for diagnosing every modern crisis. Notice both the people's repeated turning and the Lord's compassion when they groan.

days.observationQuestion: What changes after Joshua's generation, and why does the Lord raise judges?
days.reflectionQuestion: What practices might help a community remember God's acts across generations?
days.prayer: Lord, keep us from forgetting Your mercy and turning from You.

days.context: Famine takes Naomi's family to Moab, where her husband and sons die. Returning toward Bethlehem, Naomi urges her daughters-in-law to remain; Ruth chooses to stay with her.

devotional.title: Loyalty beside grief
devotional.body: Ruth's loyalty is real, and Naomi's bitterness is also real. Do not use Ruth's choice to tell grieving people how quickly to feel hopeful. The chapter ends at barley harvest, before the story's outcome is known.

days.observationQuestion: What losses does Naomi name, and what distinct choices do Ruth and Orpah make?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you offer loyal presence without trying to correct someone's grief?
days.prayer: Lord, stay near those who grieve and make me a faithful companion.

days.context: Boaz acts at the town gate to redeem family property and marry Ruth. The women bless Naomi, and the genealogy closes by connecting their family to David.

devotional.title: Ruth and Naomi receive a future
devotional.body: The story honours Ruth's loyal care and Boaz's public responsibility. It should not be reduced to a promise that every faithful widow will remarry or have a child; the ending locates ordinary kindness within Israel's larger story.

days.observationQuestion: What does Boaz do publicly, what do the women say to Naomi, and where does the genealogy lead?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might reliable care for a vulnerable neighbour take a practical form?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me faithful kindness in ordinary responsibilities.

days.context: David proposes to build a temple, but through Nathan the Lord recounts what He has done and promises to establish David's house and kingdom. David answers in prayer.

devotional.title: The Lord promises David a house
devotional.body: The promise concerns David's line and Israel's kingdom, not a blank cheque for any leader's plans. Christian readers trace royal hope toward Jesus while first hearing David's surprise that God would establish his house.

days.observationQuestion: What does David propose, what does the Lord promise instead, and how does David pray?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might gratitude be a better response than trying to secure your own legacy?
days.prayer: Lord, keep me humble before Your faithful purposes.

days.context: The ark enters the new temple, the Lord's glory fills it, and Solomon prays for Israel and for foreigners who come seeking the Lord. He repeatedly asks God to hear from heaven.

devotional.title: The temple is dedicated
devotional.body: The temple is a place for the Lord's name, not a building that contains Him. Solomon's prayer anticipates sin and exile as well as worship; do not skip its calls for forgiveness and justice.

days.observationQuestion: Where does Solomon say God dwells, and for whom does he ask God to hear and act?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might worship hold together God's nearness, holiness, and concern for outsiders?
days.prayer: Lord, hear Your people and teach us justice and welcome.

days.context: Psalm 23 portrays the Lord as shepherd and host. The speaker receives guidance and provision, walks through a dark valley, and trusts the Lord's presence even near enemies.

devotional.title: The Shepherd's care
devotional.body: The psalm does not promise a path without danger. Its comfort rests in the Shepherd who remains with the speaker through the valley and welcomes him to the table.

days.observationQuestion: Which images show care, and where does danger still appear within the psalm?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need the Shepherd's guidance or comfort?
days.prayer: Shepherding Lord, guide me and help me trust Your presence in the valley.

days.context: Psalm 51's heading places this prayer after Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba. David asks for mercy, cleansing, a renewed heart, and restored joy while acknowledging his sin.

devotional.title: Asking for a clean heart
devotional.body: The plea for forgiveness must not erase the harm done to Bathsheba or the consequences narrated in 2 Samuel 12. Repentance tells the truth and seeks changed conduct.

days.observationQuestion: What wrong does David confess, what renewal does he seek, and what kind of heart does God welcome?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need God's mercy and renewal?
days.prayer: Merciful God, make me truthful about my sin and ready to turn from harm.

days.context: Isaiah 9 speaks of light for people in darkness and a child associated with righteous rule. The chapter then turns to a repeated warning about judgment on Israel's pride and injustice.

devotional.title: Light amid judgment
devotional.body: Christians hear the royal child in relation to Jesus, but the promised reign should not be detached from Isaiah's setting or used to skip the chapter's warnings. Read both hope and judgment.

days.observationQuestion: What changes in verses 1-7, and what actions bring warning in the rest of the chapter?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the promise of just rule challenge the ways people misuse power?
days.prayer: Lord, give me hope in Your justice and ears for Your warning.

days.context: Isaiah pictures a shoot from Jesse, endowed with the Lord's Spirit, judging with righteousness, and bringing a peace that reaches creation and the nations.

devotional.title: A ruler from Jesse's line
devotional.body: The vision grows from David's line but reaches beyond ordinary human rule. Christian readers see the Messiah in this promised ruler; the chapter's concern for the poor and its future hope should remain visible.

days.observationQuestion: What qualities mark the ruler, and who benefits from his just judgment?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where does longing for righteous rule sharpen your care for those treated unfairly?
days.prayer: Lord, bring Your just peace and teach me to seek it faithfully.

days.context: Isaiah's Servant is rejected, bears others' iniquities, and is later vindicated. Read the chapter with the surrounding Servant passage in Isaiah 52:13-53:12 in view.

devotional.title: The suffering Servant
devotional.body: The poem links the Servant's suffering with the wrongdoing of others rather than celebrating suffering for its own sake. Christians read it in light of Jesus' death and resurrection (see Acts 8:32-35); that connection should be explained, not assumed or used to excuse harm.

days.observationQuestion: What does the passage say the Servant suffers, for whom, and what follows his suffering?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the Servant's bearing of others' wrongdoing invite gratitude without asking the harmed to remain unsafe?
days.prayer: Lord, help me read the Servant's suffering with humility and hope.

days.context: Isaiah invites the thirsty to receive without price, recalls the Lord's covenant faithfulness, calls the wicked to turn, and compares God's effective word to rain and snow.

devotional.title: An open invitation to receive
devotional.body: The invitation is grounded in the Lord's mercy and promise, not in a claim that every desire will be supplied on demand. Read the call to seek and return alongside the joyful imagery at the end.

days.observationQuestion: What is freely offered, what response is called for, and what does God's word accomplish?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might returning to God matter more than trying to purchase security?
days.prayer: Merciful Lord, draw me to Your word and teach me to return.

days.context: Jeremiah speaks hope to Israel and Judah amid judgment and displacement. The chapter promises return, mourning turned toward joy, and a new covenant in which God's instruction is written on hearts.

devotional.title: Hope for a scattered people
devotional.body: The new covenant promise in verses 31-34 is addressed to the houses of Israel and Judah. Christian readers connect it with Jesus, but should not erase its first audience or treat restoration as instant relief for every sorrow.

days.observationQuestion: Who is promised a new covenant, and how does it differ from the broken covenant?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does God's commitment to forgive shape your hope without rushing grief?
days.prayer: Lord, make me attentive to Your faithful promise and forgiving mercy.

days.context: The poem speaks from affliction after Jerusalem's devastation. In the middle of grief it remembers the Lord's mercies, then returns to sorrow, injustice, and a plea for God to see.

devotional.title: Hope voiced within lament
devotional.body: The words about renewed mercy in verses 21-24 do not cancel the poem's pain. Read the whole chapter before using those verses to comfort someone else; lament and hope remain together here.

days.observationQuestion: What suffering is described before and after verses 21-24, and what does the writer ask God to see?
days.reflectionQuestion: Can you leave room for honest grief while recalling mercy?
days.prayer: Merciful Lord, see those who suffer and keep hope alive without silencing lament.

days.context: Ezekiel addresses Israel in exile. The Lord promises restoration, cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit, while explaining that He acts for the honour of His name.

devotional.title: A new heart for exiles
devotional.body: This is a promise to a displaced people within Israel's history, not a formula for claiming anyone else's land or a guarantee of immediate personal success. Notice that renewal includes a changed heart and life, not merely changed circumstances.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord say He will do in verses 22-27, and why does He say He acts?
days.reflectionQuestion: What kind of inward change is more important than outward success?
days.prayer: Lord, cleanse my heart and lead me toward faithful living.

days.context: In exile, Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones brought to life by the Lord's word and breath. A second sign with two sticks points toward the reunification of God's people under one shepherd.

devotional.title: Dry bones and a reunited people
devotional.body: The Lord Himself interprets the bones as the whole house of Israel in despair. Do not reduce the vision to a motivational promise that any personal project will revive. Hear its hope for a people who think their future is cut off.

days.observationQuestion: Who are the bones according to verses 11-14, and what does the second sign promise?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you speak hope to a discouraged community without making empty guarantees?
days.prayer: Lord, breathe hope into those who feel cut off and forgotten.

days.context: Luke introduces the promised births of John and Jesus. Gabriel speaks to Zechariah and Mary, Elizabeth welcomes Mary, and two songs praise God's mercy and covenant faithfulness.

devotional.title: God remembers mercy
devotional.body: Mary's song speaks of the lowly raised and the hungry filled, while Zechariah speaks of God's remembered promises to Abraham. These births belong to Israel's story and God's rescue, not a general promise that every longing for a child will be met in the same way.

days.observationQuestion: What is announced about each child, and which acts of God do Mary and Zechariah praise?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might remembering mercy change the way you worship amid waiting?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to praise Your mercy and honour those still waiting.

days.context: Matthew opens with a genealogy linking Jesus to Abraham and David, then tells how Joseph receives the news of Mary's pregnancy and a command to name the child Jesus.

devotional.title: Jesus enters Israel's story
devotional.body: The genealogy places Jesus in a real family history with complicated lives. The angel says He will save His people from their sins, and Matthew names Him Immanuel. Read both His human lineage and His saving mission.

days.observationQuestion: Which ancestors are named, and what do the names Jesus and Immanuel explain?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does a long, imperfect family story shape your view of God's faithfulness?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me receive Your saving presence with gratitude.

days.context: Luke sets Jesus' birth under an imperial census and places Mary and Joseph in Bethlehem. Shepherds hear the angelic announcement; later, Simeon and Anna speak over the child in the temple.

devotional.title: The Savior is born
devotional.body: Luke holds humble circumstances alongside the announcement of a Savior. The shepherds' witness and the temple voices connect this child's arrival to Israel's hope; do not reduce the chapter to a peaceful scene without its wider promises.

days.observationQuestion: Who hears about Jesus, what titles or hopes are spoken, and how do they respond?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does Luke's choice of witnesses draw your attention to about Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me receive the news of Your coming with wonder and faith.

days.context: After His baptism, Jesus resists temptation in the wilderness, then reads Isaiah in Nazareth and speaks of good news to the poor. The chapter ends with teaching, healing, and His insistence on proclaiming the kingdom elsewhere.

devotional.title: Jesus announces His mission
devotional.body: Jesus' Nazareth listeners move from admiration to anger when He recalls God's mercy beyond Israel. Do not turn the Isaiah reading into a promise that every hardship ends immediately; notice Jesus' announcement, rejection, and continuing mission.

days.observationQuestion: How does Jesus answer temptation, what does He announce in Nazareth, and why do the listeners become angry?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which part of Jesus' mission challenges what you expected Him to do?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me hear Your good news and follow You beyond my expectations.

days.context: Jesus begins the Sermon on the Mount by blessing unlikely people, calling disciples salt and light, and addressing the heart beneath commands about anger, desire, truth, retaliation, and enemies.

devotional.title: The King's opening teaching
devotional.body: The Beatitudes describe life under God's kingdom, not a checklist for earning it. Jesus deepens rather than discards God's law. Read His difficult examples as a call to whole-hearted righteousness, not permission for others to abuse you.

days.observationQuestion: Who does Jesus call blessed, and how does He move from outward acts to the heart?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might peacemaking or truthfulness require a concrete change?
days.prayer: King Jesus, shape my heart and actions in Your way.

days.context: Jesus continues the Sermon on the Mount with teaching on giving, prayer, fasting, treasure, and worry. He repeatedly points disciples to their Father rather than to public approval.

devotional.title: Life before the Father
devotional.body: The Lord's Prayer joins God's name and kingdom with daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance. Jesus' words about anxiety invite trust; they should not shame people struggling with poverty or illness.

days.observationQuestion: What does Jesus say about being seen by others, and what needs does the Lord's Prayer name?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where could attention to the Father free you from performing for an audience?
days.prayer: Father, provide what I need and teach me to seek Your kingdom.

days.context: Jesus teaches through parables about hearing and receiving the word, then crosses the lake with His disciples and stills a storm. The chapter moves from hidden growth to a question about His authority.

devotional.title: Hear the word and watch the storm
devotional.body: The soils invite self-examination without making growth a measure of personal worth. In the boat, frightened disciples meet Jesus' authority over the wind; the scene does not promise believers a life without storms.

days.observationQuestion: What hinders the word in the soil parable, and what do the disciples ask after the storm?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you listen patiently while entrusting fear to Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, open my ears to Your word and meet me in fear.

days.context: After feeding a crowd and healing a blind man in stages, Jesus hears Peter confess that He is the Christ. Jesus then predicts His suffering and calls followers to take up the cross.

devotional.title: Seeing the Messiah clearly
devotional.body: Peter can name Jesus rightly and still resist the path Jesus describes. Read the call to self-denial in the light of Jesus' own suffering, not as a demand to stay in abuse or neglect ordinary responsibilities.

days.observationQuestion: What does Peter confess, what does Jesus predict, and why does He correct Peter?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do your expectations of Jesus need to be shaped by His words?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, teach me to follow Your way with wisdom and courage.

days.context: Jesus speaks these parables while tax collectors and sinners draw near and religious critics object to His welcome. Read the lost sheep, lost coin, and two sons within that conversation.

devotional.title: Joy over the lost
devotional.body: Each story presses the joy of finding what was lost. The final parable also leaves the elder son's response open, turning the critics' complaint back on them. Notice the father's welcome without flattening the younger son's wrongdoing or the elder son's resentment.

days.observationQuestion: What prompts Jesus to tell these stories, and who rejoices or refuses to join the joy?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might you need to receive mercy or welcome another's return?
days.prayer: Merciful Father, help me rejoice in Your grace without hiding my need for it.

days.context: Jesus welcomes Zacchaeus and speaks of seeking the lost. A parable addresses expectations of an immediate kingdom, and His entry into Jerusalem leads to tears over the city and action in the temple.

devotional.title: The King draws near
devotional.body: Zacchaeus' restitution shows that welcome and changed conduct belong together. The crowd's celebration and Jesus' weeping should both be heard before reducing this chapter to a triumphal procession.

days.observationQuestion: How does Zacchaeus respond to Jesus, and what does Jesus say and do as He approaches Jerusalem?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could receiving mercy lead to a concrete act of repair?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me welcome Your mercy and respond honestly.

days.context: Lazarus dies before Jesus arrives. Martha and Mary speak to Him from grief, Jesus weeps, and He calls Lazarus from the tomb. The sign also intensifies the leaders' plan against Jesus.

devotional.title: Jesus meets grief at Lazarus's tomb
devotional.body: Jesus' promise of resurrection does not make the sisters' sorrow unreal; He enters it. Lazarus's return is a sign pointing to Jesus, not a guarantee that every death will be reversed now.

days.observationQuestion: What do the sisters say, how does Jesus respond to their grief, and what follows the sign?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might Jesus' presence with mourners shape the way you comfort someone?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, meet us in grief and hold us in resurrection hope.

days.context: On the night before His death, Jesus washes His disciples' feet, speaks of betrayal and departure, and gives them a new command to love one another.

devotional.title: The Lord serves His friends
devotional.body: The foot washing is an act of the Lord who knows where He came from and where He is going. Service follows His love; it must not be used to require the vulnerable to accept exploitation.

days.observationQuestion: What does Jesus know before He washes feet, and what command does He give after Judas leaves?
days.reflectionQuestion: What humble act of care could reflect His love without ignoring healthy boundaries?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, teach me to receive Your care and love others faithfully.

days.context: John 19 follows Jesus' arrest and trial. Notice the royal language, the people present at the cross, Jesus' words before death, and the care taken in His burial.

devotional.title: The crucified King
devotional.body: John presents Jesus' real suffering and death without turning the cross into a mere example of courage. His final cry belongs in the scene of His completed work; the burial confirms that He truly died. Read this chapter before moving to the resurrection witnesses in John 20.

days.observationQuestion: What words and actions frame Jesus as King, and what does John report about His death and burial?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does staying with the whole crucifixion account affect your response to Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me face Your cross with gratitude, reverence, and honesty.

days.context: Luke recounts Jesus before Pilate and Herod, His crucifixion among criminals, His death, and His burial. Leaders and soldiers mock Him while others grieve or speak on His behalf.

devotional.title: Jesus suffers under human injustice
devotional.body: The chapter shows both Jesus' innocence and His real suffering. Do not rush from the cross to Easter or use His endurance to excuse injustice against others. Notice His words of mercy and the witnesses to His death.

days.observationQuestion: Who declares Jesus innocent, what does He say from the cross, and who witnesses His death?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does staying with Luke's account affect your gratitude and concern for the unjustly treated?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me face Your suffering with honesty and reverence.

days.context: John 20 moves from the empty tomb to Mary's encounter, Jesus' appearance to the gathered disciples, and Thomas' confession. John states his purpose in verses 30-31.

devotional.title: Witnesses to the risen Jesus
devotional.body: The witnesses do not all begin with instant understanding. Mary, the disciples, and Thomas encounter the risen Jesus in distinct scenes. John's stated aim is that readers believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name.

days.observationQuestion: What does each witness see or hear, and what purpose does John give for recording these signs?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which witness's movement toward belief would you like to read more slowly?
days.prayer: Risen Lord Jesus, lead me from hearing the witnesses to trusting You.

days.context: Women find the tomb empty; Jesus meets two travellers on the Emmaus road and later appears to the gathered disciples. He explains His suffering and resurrection in the light of Scripture.

devotional.title: The risen Jesus opens the Scriptures
devotional.body: The witnesses move through fear, confusion, recognition, and joy. Luke does not ask readers to pretend they understood at once. The risen Jesus sends His followers to proclaim repentance and forgiveness.

days.observationQuestion: What do the women report, how do the travellers recognise Jesus, and what mission does He give?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which witness's movement toward understanding would you like to read more slowly?
days.prayer: Risen Lord, open the Scriptures and steady my faith in Your witness.

days.context: At Pentecost the Spirit enables witness; Peter explains the event by speaking of Jesus' death, resurrection, and exaltation. The crowd asks how to respond, and the chapter ends with the shared life of the new believers.

devotional.title: The Spirit and the first believers
devotional.body: Acts 2 links the Spirit's gift to testimony about the risen Jesus, a call to repent and be baptized, and a community devoted to teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer. Observe these parts together rather than reducing the chapter to a single dramatic moment.

days.observationQuestion: What does Peter say God has done with Jesus, how do hearers respond, and what practices mark the new community?
days.reflectionQuestion: What part of the church's shared life in verses 42-47 invites a concrete step of participation?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, make me attentive to Your Spirit, Your gospel, and the life of Your people.

days.context: Saul travels to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus. The risen Lord confronts him; Ananias receives a difficult call to welcome him. The chapter also follows Peter's ministry.

devotional.title: Saul is stopped and sent
devotional.body: Saul's reversal is Jesus' initiative, not proof that every persecutor changes quickly or should immediately be trusted. Ananias' fear is named, and Saul's new witness meets opposition. Follow the whole chapter beyond the road scene.

days.observationQuestion: What does Jesus say to Saul and Ananias, and how does Saul's public message change?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you remain open to grace while taking another person's safety seriously?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, turn hearts toward You and give Your people discernment.

days.context: Cornelius and Peter each receive a vision. Peter comes to a Gentile household, proclaims Jesus' life, death, and resurrection, and sees the Spirit given while he is speaking.

devotional.title: The gospel reaches Cornelius
devotional.body: Peter learns that he must not treat these Gentile hearers as unclean or exclude them from hearing the gospel. The Spirit's gift surprises Jewish believers who came with him. Follow Peter's message about Jesus as well as the crossing of a social boundary.

days.observationQuestion: What does Peter say about Jesus in verses 34-43, and what surprises those with him in verses 44-48?
days.reflectionQuestion: Who might you wrongly assume is beyond hearing the good news?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, keep me from favouritism and make me ready to share Your good news.

days.context: A dispute over circumcision brings Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem. Peter, James, and the assembly discuss Gentile inclusion, send a letter, and later Paul and Barnabas separate over Mark.

devotional.title: Grace for Gentile believers
devotional.body: Peter says salvation comes through the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by placing Israel's law on Gentile converts as a condition of rescue. The letter addresses shared life in a mixed community. Do not miss the unresolved human disagreement at the chapter's end.

days.observationQuestion: What question starts the meeting, what does Peter say about grace, and what does the letter ask of Gentile believers?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can conviction and careful listening both serve a divided community?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, keep Your grace central as Your people discern together.

days.context: Paul continues his argument that both Jews and Gentiles stand accountable before God. He then announces God's righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ and says boasting is excluded.

devotional.title: God's righteousness and human need
devotional.body: The chapter's charge of universal sin prepares for the good news of grace; it is not a licence to single out one group as worse. Justification is God's gift in Christ, not a reward for flawless law-keeping.

days.observationQuestion: How does Paul describe human accountability, and what changes in verses 21-26?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might grace replace boasting or despair in your response to God?
days.prayer: Righteous God, thank You for mercy in Christ rather than confidence in myself.

days.context: Romans 8 follows Paul's account of sin, law, and life in Christ. It moves from no condemnation through adoption and groaning to the Spirit's help and God's inseparable love.

devotional.title: Life in the Spirit and hope in suffering
devotional.body: Paul does not deny suffering: creation groans, believers groan, and the Spirit helps in weakness. The final assurance belongs with these honest descriptions, not in place of them.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Spirit do in verses 1-17 and 26-27, and what cannot separate believers from Christ's love?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which part of this chapter helps you pray amid weakness rather than hide it?
days.prayer: Father, hold me in Christ's love and help me by Your Spirit.

days.context: Paul describes people dead in wrongdoing, made alive with Christ by grace, and created for good works. He then turns to Jews and Gentiles brought near and reconciled in one body.

devotional.title: Grace makes one new people
devotional.body: Verses 8-10 keep salvation as gift and good works as its fruit. Do not stop there: Christ also breaks down hostility and builds a shared dwelling for God. Grace changes belonging as well as conduct.

days.observationQuestion: What does God do in verses 4-10, and what does Christ make of those once far apart?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where could gratitude for grace become an act of welcome or peace?
days.prayer: God of mercy, make me alive in Christ and ready to welcome His people.

days.context: Paul urges a divided community toward humility and shared concern, points to Christ's self-giving and exaltation, then commends Timothy and Epaphroditus as examples of care.

devotional.title: The mind of Christ among His people
devotional.body: Christ's humility is the basis of Paul's appeal, not a command to erase your worth or tolerate harm. Notice that God exalts Jesus and that the chapter ends with concrete coworkers who serve others.

days.observationQuestion: What movement is described in verses 5-11, and how do Timothy and Epaphroditus embody concern for others?
days.reflectionQuestion: What could humble care look like in a relationship where you have real responsibility?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, form Your generous mind in me and in Your church.

days.context: John's vision follows the judgment scenes of Revelation 20. Chapter 21 pictures a new heaven and earth, the holy city, God's dwelling with His people, and the removal of death and tears.

devotional.title: God dwells with His people
devotional.body: This is a vision of God's future renewal, not a promise that present grief has already ended. Its centre is God's presence with His people. Hold the hope of verses 1-5 alongside the chapter's call to faithful endurance rather than using it to rush another person's sorrow.

days.observationQuestion: What does John see in verses 1-5, and what does the voice say God will do?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can future hope make room for honest grief and faithful living now?
days.prayer: God of hope, keep me near You in present sorrow as I await Your promised renewal.

days.context: John's final vision follows the new creation of chapter 21. The river and tree of life appear, God's servants see His face, and Jesus promises to come; the book closes with invitation and warning.

devotional.title: The river of life and the final invitation
devotional.body: The closing hope centres on God's presence and healing for the nations. Do not use its images to calculate a date for Jesus' return. Hear the repeated invitation to come and the final prayer for His coming.

days.observationQuestion: What is restored in verses 1-5, and who is invited in verses 16-21?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might future healing deepen patient faithfulness now?
days.prayer: Come, Lord Jesus. Keep my hope awake and my welcome wide.

plans.title: Old Testament Story in 60 Days
plans.description: Selected chapters introduce the Old Testament's story, worship, wisdom and prophetic hope.
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: 60 selected chapters, not every chapter of the Bible.
plans.purpose: To give a manageable overview before choosing where to study more deeply.
plans.bestFor: Seeing the big picture before deeper study
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Genesis opens with God speaking, ordering, and blessing creation. Humanity, male and female, is made in God's image and given a vocation within the world He calls good.

devotional.title: God creates and blesses
devotional.body: The chapter begins with God's initiative, not human achievement. Its repeated goodness grounds human dignity and responsibility; it does not answer every modern question about the mechanics of creation.

days.observationQuestion: What does God make, bless, and call good, and what task is given to humanity?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might shared image-bearing dignity change the way you regard another person?
days.prayer: Creator God, teach me to receive Your world with gratitude and care.

days.context: Genesis 2 draws close to the human scene: the Lord forms the man, plants a garden, gives work and a boundary, and makes a fitting partner. The chapter ends with union and openness.

devotional.title: Life in the garden
devotional.body: Read this alongside Genesis 1 rather than treating the two chapters as competing stories. The human vocation includes cultivation and care; the boundary reminds the reader that freedom is lived before God.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord give the humans, and what limit does He set?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where does receiving life as gift change your sense of work or relationship?
days.prayer: Lord, help me tend what You entrust to me with gratitude.

days.context: Genesis 3 follows the good creation and human vocation of Genesis 1-2. The serpent disputes God's word; the man and woman disobey, hide, and blame. Read the chapter's judgments and God's care for them together.

devotional.title: Trust broken in the garden
devotional.body: The story names a rupture with God, with one another, and with the ground. God questions the pair and announces consequences; He also clothes them before they leave the garden. Do not skip either human responsibility or God's continued care.

days.observationQuestion: How do the serpent, woman, and man each speak about God's command, and what changes after they eat?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where does this chapter help you name mistrust or blame truthfully rather than hide it?
days.prayer: Lord, help me hear Your word, own my wrongdoing, and seek Your mercy.

days.context: Genesis 6 describes human wickedness and violence, the Lord's grief, and His command for Noah to build an ark and preserve living creatures.

devotional.title: Corruption and Noah's calling
devotional.body: The chapter's opening verses are difficult and have more than one interpretation; do not make speculation about them the centre. The passage explicitly names violence and corruption, then records the Lord's decision and Noah's obedience.

days.observationQuestion: What does the chapter say God sees, and what is Noah told to do?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the text's concern with violence shape your reading of judgment?
days.prayer: Lord, guard us from violence and teach us to heed Your word.

days.context: After the flood, God blesses Noah's family and makes a covenant with them and every living creature. The chapter also records Noah's failure and its effect on his family.

devotional.title: A covenant after the flood
devotional.body: The rainbow marks God's promise not to destroy all flesh by flood again. This is a covenant with living creatures, not a guarantee that no local flood or human evil will occur. Hold the promise and the chapter's sober ending together.

days.observationQuestion: Who receives the covenant in verses 8-17, and what exactly is promised?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does God's care for living creatures affect the way you receive this promise?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You for Your patience with a wounded world.

days.context: After the scattering at Babel, the Lord calls Abram to leave his country and promises land, descendants, and blessing that will reach all families of the earth.

devotional.title: Abram is called
devotional.body: The story begins with God's initiative and Abram's journey. Read the promise to Abram in its own setting before tracing how later Scripture understands blessing for the nations.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord command Abram, what does He promise, and how does Abram respond?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might God's purpose to bless others shape the way you read the rest of this story?
days.prayer: Lord, help me hear Your call and trust Your faithful purposes.
