days.context: Abram worries because he remains childless. The Lord answers with a promise about descendants, and the chapter closes with a covenant concerning land and a future that includes hardship.

devotional.title: Promise amid waiting
devotional.body: Abram believes the Lord, and the Lord counts it to him as righteousness. The promise does not mean the wait or coming suffering vanishes. Keep God's specific covenant with Abram distinct from a guarantee about every reader's wishes.

days.observationQuestion: What concern does Abram bring, and what does the Lord promise in verses 1-6 and 13-18?
days.reflectionQuestion: What do Abram's honest questions teach you about bringing uncertainty before God?
days.prayer: Faithful Lord, teach me to trust You without demanding that my waiting follow Abram's story.

days.context: The Lord reaffirms His covenant with Abram, changes Abram's and Sarai's names, appoints circumcision as its sign, and promises a son through Sarah.

devotional.title: The covenant marked in a family
devotional.body: The promise is given to this family within a long wait; it is not a guarantee of a child for every reader. Notice Sarah's named place in the promise and the difference between God's word about Isaac and Abraham's concern for Ishmael.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord promise, what sign is commanded, and how are Sarah and Ishmael addressed?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does this chapter hold promise and long waiting together?
days.prayer: Faithful Lord, help me honour Your promises without claiming another family's story as my own.

days.context: Genesis 22 describes a specific test of Abraham after the promised birth of Isaac. The messenger stops Abraham, forbids harm to the boy, and a ram is provided in his place.

devotional.title: The Lord provides
devotional.body: This disturbing account must not be turned into a pattern for harming a child or obeying a private impression to do so. Attend to God's interruption, the provision, and the renewed promise to Abraham before drawing later Christian connections.

days.observationQuestion: Who stops Abraham in verses 11-12, what is provided, and what promise follows?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the text's refusal of Isaac's death shape your reading of the test?
days.prayer: Lord, keep me attentive to Your word and protective of those entrusted to my care.

days.context: Isaac sends Jacob away, and at Bethel Jacob dreams of a stairway between earth and heaven. The Lord repeats the family promise and pledges to be with him; Jacob wakes in awe and makes a vow.

devotional.title: Jacob meets God on the road
devotional.body: Jacob receives this promise while away from home after a troubled family story. God's specific land and offspring promise is not a general guarantee that every journey will go safely.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord promise Jacob, and how does Jacob respond when he wakes?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might awe change the way you notice God's care without claiming Jacob's promise as your own?
days.prayer: Lord, keep me attentive to Your presence and faithful word.

days.context: Joseph's dreams, Jacob's favouritism, and the brothers' jealousy lead to Joseph being sold and Jacob being deceived. The chapter also names Reuben's and Judah's different actions.

devotional.title: Joseph's dreams and his brothers' betrayal
devotional.body: The later good God brings from Joseph's story does not make the brothers' violence harmless. Read the family conflict and Joseph's vulnerability honestly before moving to the reconciliation chapters.

days.observationQuestion: What fuels the brothers' anger, and what does each brother do when Joseph is in danger?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can naming jealousy early prevent harm to someone with less power?
days.prayer: Lord, expose envy in me and make me protective of the vulnerable.

days.context: After years of separation and hardship, Joseph tells his brothers who he is. He names their sale of him into Egypt and describes how God has preserved life through the famine.

devotional.title: Joseph reveals himself
devotional.body: Joseph's account of providence does not make his brothers' betrayal good or require every harmed person to reconcile quickly. Observe his tears, their fear, and the practical provision for the family.

days.observationQuestion: What wrong does Joseph name, what purpose does he see, and how does he provide for his family?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can hope for good avoid denying a real wrong?
days.prayer: Lord, help me tell the truth about harm and notice Your care.

days.context: After Jacob dies, Joseph mourns and buries him. His brothers fear revenge; Joseph answers by distinguishing their evil intent from the good God brought about, and he speaks of God's future care for Israel.

devotional.title: Grief, fear, and a future promise
devotional.body: Joseph's words do not call the brothers' actions good or require victims to offer instant trust. The book ends with Joseph's death in Egypt and a hope that God will bring the family onward.

days.observationQuestion: What do the brothers fear, what does Joseph say about their intent, and what hope ends the book?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you hold hope for God's good without denying wrongdoing or grief?
days.prayer: Lord, meet us in grief and keep us truthful about both harm and hope.

days.context: After Joseph's generation, a new Pharaoh fears Israel's growth and imposes forced labour. Midwives refuse his command to kill Hebrew boys, and the chapter ends with further violence.

devotional.title: Israel grows under oppression
devotional.body: Israel's fruitfulness does not prevent suffering. The midwives' courage is concrete resistance to an unjust order; read their action without treating danger to oppressed people as a simple test of faith.

days.observationQuestion: What fears drive Pharaoh's policies, and how do the midwives respond?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where can you protect a vulnerable person without romanticising the risk they face?
days.prayer: Lord, defend the oppressed and give courage to those protecting life.

days.context: While Moses tends a flock, the Lord speaks from the burning bush. He names the suffering of Israel in Egypt, recalls the ancestors' covenant, and sends Moses to Pharaoh.

devotional.title: The Lord sees and sends
devotional.body: God's holy presence begins this rescue, and Moses' objections remain part of the conversation. The divine name is given in the setting of covenant faithfulness, not as a technique for mastering God.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord say He has seen and heard, and how does Moses respond to being sent?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could attending to another person's suffering change the way you pray or act?
days.prayer: Holy Lord, help me listen to Your word and care for those who suffer.

days.context: After Pharaoh increases Israel's burden, the Lord repeats His promise to bring them out, take them as His people, and bring them to the promised land. A genealogy then locates Moses and Aaron within Israel.

devotional.title: A promise to a discouraged people
devotional.body: The people cannot listen because of broken spirit and hard labour. Their exhaustion is not presented as a moral failure. God's covenant words precede the visible change in their circumstances.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord say He will do, and why do the people struggle to hear Moses?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you speak hope without dismissing someone's exhaustion?
days.prayer: Lord, remember those worn down by labour and keep Your word before them.

days.context: The Lord gives Israel instructions for the Passover while they are still in Egypt. Households mark their doors, share a meal, and prepare to leave; the chapter also records judgment and the beginning of the exodus.

devotional.title: Passover and deliverance
devotional.body: Passover belongs first to Israel's rescue from slavery and its remembered worship. Its details are not instructions for Christians to imitate the doorpost ritual. Read the commanded remembrance and costly deliverance before tracing later connections to Christ.

days.observationQuestion: What are Israelite households told to do, and how is this night to be remembered?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does this account show about rescue and remembrance without making it a promise of exemption from all danger?
days.prayer: Lord, help me remember Your saving acts with reverence and gratitude.

days.context: With Pharaoh's army approaching, Israel fears for its life. The Lord tells Moses to lead them forward, divides the sea, and brings the people through while the pursuing force is overwhelmed.

devotional.title: A way through the sea
devotional.body: This is Israel's particular deliverance from slavery and pursuit, not a guarantee that every danger ends in escape. Read the people's fear, the Lord's action, and the costly judgment together.

days.observationQuestion: How do the people and Moses speak at the sea, and what does the Lord do?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can this story lead to gratitude for rescue without making light of current danger?
days.prayer: Delivering Lord, hear those in danger and teach me reverent trust.

days.context: After leaving Egypt, Israel complains of hunger. The Lord provides manna and quail, instructs daily gathering, and establishes a pattern of rest on the seventh day.

devotional.title: Bread in the wilderness
devotional.body: The hunger is real, and God's provision meets a community in need. This account describes Israel's wilderness life; it is not a promise that no believer will ever face food insecurity. Notice the limits on hoarding and the provision for rest.

days.observationQuestion: What is provided, how is it gathered, and what changes on the sixth and seventh days?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could daily dependence and shared provision shape care for hungry neighbours?
days.prayer: Lord, provide for those without enough and teach us generous trust.

days.context: At Sinai, the Lord recalls carrying Israel out of Egypt and calls them to be His treasured people. Moses prepares the community, and the mountain scene stresses God's holiness and boundaries.

devotional.title: Israel prepares to meet the Lord
devotional.body: The covenant invitation follows deliverance; Israel does not earn rescue by first becoming holy. The limits around the mountain protect the people and frame the commandments that follow.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord recall doing for Israel, and how are the people told to prepare?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does gratitude for prior rescue change the way you hear a call to obedience?
days.prayer: Holy Lord, help me receive Your word with gratitude and reverence.

days.context: Israel has been rescued from Egypt before the commandments are spoken at Sinai. The chapter begins by naming the Lord as their deliverer, then addresses worship, family, speech, rest, and neighbourly conduct.

devotional.title: A covenant people learn to live
devotional.body: The commandments form covenant life for a redeemed people; they are not a ladder by which Israel first earns rescue. Notice both devotion to God and responsibility toward neighbours as you read.

days.observationQuestion: How does the Lord introduce Himself in verses 1-2, and which commands address life with neighbours?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where would truthful worship change the way you treat another person?
days.prayer: Delivering Lord, teach me to honour You and love my neighbours faithfully.

days.context: While Moses is on Sinai, Aaron makes a golden calf and the people worship it. The Lord names their betrayal; Moses intercedes and confronts the community.

devotional.title: The calf and Moses' intercession
devotional.body: This chapter is a grave account of idolatry and judgment, including violence that should not be imitated. Read Moses' appeal to God's promise alongside the harm of worship fashioned to suit human impatience.

days.observationQuestion: What do the people ask Aaron to make, and what does Moses appeal to when he prays?
days.reflectionQuestion: What can impatience reveal about the things you are tempted to trust?
days.prayer: Lord, turn me from false security and keep me faithful to You.

days.context: Exodus 34 follows Israel's golden calf and Moses' intercession. The Lord renews the covenant and reveals His character while warning Israel against idolatry.

devotional.title: Mercy after the broken covenant
devotional.body: God's mercy does not call the calf harmless, and His justice does not erase His compassion. Read His self-description in verses 6-7 alongside the covenant renewal rather than lifting one phrase out of the story.

days.observationQuestion: How does the Lord describe Himself, and what commands accompany the renewed covenant?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need to receive both God's mercy and His call to faithfulness?
days.prayer: Merciful Lord, keep me from treating Your patience lightly.

days.context: The Lord addresses Israel's congregation through Moses. This chapter places worship, family, economic practices, justice, and care for neighbours under the call to be holy.

devotional.title: Holiness in ordinary life
devotional.body: These are covenant instructions to Israel, not a set of isolated rules for earning God's favour. Gleaning, honest judgment, and care for the resident foreigner show that holiness includes how vulnerable neighbours are treated.

days.observationQuestion: Which commands in verses 9-18 and 33-34 protect a neighbour from exploitation?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might love of neighbour require a more concrete act of fairness?
days.prayer: Holy Lord, teach me to honour You in the way I treat others.

days.context: After the spies' report in Numbers 13, Israel fears the inhabitants of the land and proposes returning to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb urge trust; Moses intercedes when judgment is announced.

devotional.title: Fear at the edge of the land
devotional.body: The chapter does not praise reckless confidence. It exposes a refusal to trust after repeated deliverance, records Moses' appeal to God's mercy, and shows consequences for that generation. Read the later failed attack after God's warning as part of the same account.

days.observationQuestion: How do the people, Joshua and Caleb, and Moses respond to the report and to God's word?
days.reflectionQuestion: What can you learn from Moses' intercession without equating your fears with Israel's land mission?
days.prayer: Lord, help me listen before fear turns me away from You.

days.context: Moses addresses Israel as they prepare to enter the land. Deuteronomy 6 calls them to hear that the Lord is one, love Him wholeheartedly, teach His words to their children, and remember His rescue from Egypt.

devotional.title: Love the Lord and remember
devotional.body: This selected chapter is not the beginning of Deuteronomy. Its call to love the Lord belongs to Israel's covenant life, including remembered deliverance and daily teaching. Read the command with its audience and story before applying its wisdom to your own worship and household.

days.observationQuestion: Who is addressed in verses 3-7, and what rescue are they told to remember in verses 20-25?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might remembering God's prior faithfulness shape what you teach or practice today?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to love You with my whole life and to remember Your faithfulness.

days.context: Moses speaks to Israel near the end of the covenant address. After naming blessing, curse, and possible exile, he speaks of return, God's compassion, and the choice set before the people.

devotional.title: A call to return and choose life
devotional.body: The promised gathering and land belong first to Israel's covenant history; they are not an individual guarantee of prosperity. Notice that God's work on the heart in verse 6 accompanies the call to love and obey Him.

days.observationQuestion: What future does Moses describe in verses 1-10, and what choice does he set before Israel in verses 15-20?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does remembering God's compassion affect your response to His call?
days.prayer: Lord, turn my heart toward love and faithful obedience.

days.context: After Moses dies, the Lord commissions Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan. He repeats the land promise, commands courage and attention to the law, and Joshua prepares the people to move.

devotional.title: Joshua receives the commission
devotional.body: The assurance of success is tied to Joshua's particular mission and Israel's covenant, not a guarantee that every project will prosper. The chapter also asks the eastern tribes to help their neighbours enter the land.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord command Joshua, and what shared responsibility is given to the eastern tribes?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could courage include faithful attention and help for others?
days.prayer: Lord, give me courage to serve faithfully within the work You entrust to me.

days.context: Joshua gathers Israel at Shechem, recounts the Lord's acts from Abraham through the land, and calls the people to put away other gods and serve the Lord.

devotional.title: Remember and choose whom to serve
devotional.body: The call to choose follows God's prior gift and rescue. Joshua also warns that covenant loyalty is serious; his words are addressed to Israel in its land, not a simple slogan detached from its history.

days.observationQuestion: Which acts of God does Joshua recount before asking the people to choose?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does remembering prior mercy add to a decision about faithfulness?
days.prayer: Lord, keep my worship rooted in gratitude and truth.

days.context: After Joshua's generation dies, Israel turns to other gods. The chapter introduces a recurring pattern: oppression, judges raised up by the Lord, temporary rescue, and renewed unfaithfulness.

devotional.title: A generation forgets
devotional.body: This is a summary of Israel's troubled life in the land, not a formula for diagnosing every modern crisis. Notice both the people's repeated turning and the Lord's compassion when they groan.

days.observationQuestion: What changes after Joshua's generation, and why does the Lord raise judges?
days.reflectionQuestion: What practices might help a community remember God's acts across generations?
days.prayer: Lord, keep us from forgetting Your mercy and turning from You.

days.context: Famine takes Naomi's family to Moab, where her husband and sons die. Returning toward Bethlehem, Naomi urges her daughters-in-law to remain; Ruth chooses to stay with her.

devotional.title: Loyalty beside grief
devotional.body: Ruth's loyalty is real, and Naomi's bitterness is also real. Do not use Ruth's choice to tell grieving people how quickly to feel hopeful. The chapter ends at barley harvest, before the story's outcome is known.

days.observationQuestion: What losses does Naomi name, and what distinct choices do Ruth and Orpah make?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you offer loyal presence without trying to correct someone's grief?
days.prayer: Lord, stay near those who grieve and make me a faithful companion.

days.context: Boaz acts at the town gate to redeem family property and marry Ruth. The women bless Naomi, and the genealogy closes by connecting their family to David.

devotional.title: Ruth and Naomi receive a future
devotional.body: The story honours Ruth's loyal care and Boaz's public responsibility. It should not be reduced to a promise that every faithful widow will remarry or have a child; the ending locates ordinary kindness within Israel's larger story.

days.observationQuestion: What does Boaz do publicly, what do the women say to Naomi, and where does the genealogy lead?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might reliable care for a vulnerable neighbour take a practical form?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me faithful kindness in ordinary responsibilities.

days.context: The boy Samuel serves at Shiloh while Eli's household is under judgment. The Lord calls Samuel and gives him a difficult message concerning Eli's family.

devotional.title: Samuel learns to hear
devotional.body: The repeated call is not a promise that every inner impression is God's voice. Samuel's first task is to receive and truthfully convey a hard word; Eli must also hear it.

days.observationQuestion: How does Samuel recognise the caller, and what message is he reluctant to give?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can attentive listening be joined to humility and truthfulness?
days.prayer: Lord, help me listen carefully and speak truth without presumption.

days.context: Samuel's sons have acted unjustly. Israel's elders ask for a king like other nations, and Samuel brings their request to the Lord.

devotional.title: Israel asks for a king
devotional.body: The elders have a real grievance, yet the Lord names a deeper rejection of His kingship. Samuel warns that a king will take people, labour, and property. Avoid treating this as a simple verdict that every form of human government is wrong.

days.observationQuestion: What reasons do the elders give, how does the Lord interpret the request, and what does Samuel warn the king will take?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can a legitimate complaint still lead to an unwise remedy?
days.prayer: Lord, give me wisdom to seek justice without making power my hope.

days.context: After Saul's rejection, the Lord sends Samuel to Jesse's family. Samuel expects an impressive older son, but the Lord chooses David and the Spirit comes upon him.

devotional.title: David is anointed
devotional.body: The contrast between outward appearance and the heart corrects Samuel's judgment. It does not grant readers the power to know another person's heart. The chapter also depicts Saul's distress and David's early service to him.

days.observationQuestion: Whom does Samuel first expect, whom does the Lord choose, and what follows the anointing?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might first impressions need to give way to patient attention?
days.prayer: Lord, correct my shallow judgments and guide me in serving well.

days.context: David proposes to build a temple, but through Nathan the Lord recounts what He has done and promises to establish David's house and kingdom. David answers in prayer.

devotional.title: The Lord promises David a house
devotional.body: The promise concerns David's line and Israel's kingdom, not a blank cheque for any leader's plans. Christian readers trace royal hope toward Jesus while first hearing David's surprise that God would establish his house.

days.observationQuestion: What does David propose, what does the Lord promise instead, and how does David pray?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might gratitude be a better response than trying to secure your own legacy?
days.prayer: Lord, keep me humble before Your faithful purposes.

days.context: Nathan's parable confronts David after his abuse of Bathsheba and killing of Uriah in 2 Samuel 11. David confesses, but the chapter also names grave consequences.

devotional.title: Nathan confronts David
devotional.body: God's mercy toward David does not erase his wrongdoing, the victims, or the harm that follows. Do not use David's confession to pressure harmed people to overlook abuse. Attend to Nathan's truth-telling and the whole chapter's grief.

days.observationQuestion: How does Nathan expose David's action, and what remains after David admits his sin?
days.reflectionQuestion: What would honest repentance require beyond saying the right words?
days.prayer: Just and merciful Lord, make me truthful about harm and ready to protect others.

days.context: The ark enters the new temple, the Lord's glory fills it, and Solomon prays for Israel and for foreigners who come seeking the Lord. He repeatedly asks God to hear from heaven.

devotional.title: The temple is dedicated
devotional.body: The temple is a place for the Lord's name, not a building that contains Him. Solomon's prayer anticipates sin and exile as well as worship; do not skip its calls for forgiveness and justice.

days.observationQuestion: Where does Solomon say God dwells, and for whom does he ask God to hear and act?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might worship hold together God's nearness, holiness, and concern for outsiders?
days.prayer: Lord, hear Your people and teach us justice and welcome.

days.context: During a severe drought, Elijah confronts Ahab and the prophets of Baal. The people witness the Lord's answer by fire, and afterward rain returns.

devotional.title: The Lord answers on Carmel
devotional.body: The chapter contrasts rival worship in Israel's crisis. Its violence against the prophets must not be copied as a model for treating religious opponents today. Notice Elijah's prayer that the people might know the Lord has turned their hearts back.

days.observationQuestion: What question does Elijah put to the people, and what does he ask in his prayer?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can loyalty to God be shown without coercion or contempt for others?
days.prayer: Lord, turn my heart toward You and make my witness peaceable.

days.context: This chapter recounts Assyria's capture of Samaria, then explains the northern kingdom's exile through a long account of covenant unfaithfulness. It also describes later peoples and mixed worship in the land.

devotional.title: Why the northern kingdom fell
devotional.body: The writer is interpreting this particular history, not giving readers permission to diagnose every modern tragedy as divine punishment. Notice the repeated warnings through prophets and the people's refusal to listen.

days.observationQuestion: What events are narrated in verses 1-6, and what reasons does the writer give in verses 7-23?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can this history call you to listen without judging another person's suffering?
days.prayer: Lord, give me ears for warning and humility before histories of loss.

days.context: Babylon besieges Jerusalem, the city suffers famine, the temple is burned, and many people are taken into exile. The final verses tell of Jehoiachin's release from prison years later.

devotional.title: Jerusalem falls
devotional.body: This is a record of devastating national loss, not a prompt to explain another person's suffering as punishment. Do not rush past the famine, destruction, and displacement to the small sign of hope at the end.

days.observationQuestion: What is lost in verses 1-21, and what changes for Jehoiachin in verses 27-30?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you honour grief while remaining open to modest signs of hope?
days.prayer: Lord, have mercy on people facing war, hunger, and displacement.

days.context: Cyrus permits exiles to return and rebuild the Lord's house in Jerusalem. Neighbours support them, and vessels taken from the temple are handed back.

devotional.title: A return from exile begins
devotional.body: The chapter marks a concrete beginning of restoration after displacement, not the end of every problem. The returning community still faces long work ahead; read the royal decree and the people's response in their historical setting.

days.observationQuestion: What does Cyrus permit, who responds, and what is returned from Babylon?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can a first step toward repair be welcomed without pretending the work is finished?
days.prayer: Lord, sustain people rebuilding after loss and make us generous in support.

days.context: After the wall is rebuilt, Ezra reads the law to the gathered people and others explain it. The people weep, are urged to celebrate and share food, and later keep the Festival of Shelters.

devotional.title: The people hear the law
devotional.body: Understanding the text is a communal task here; grief and joy both have a place. The call to share portions with those unprepared keeps celebration from becoming private comfort.

days.observationQuestion: Who helps the people understand, and what are they told to do for those without food?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could reading Scripture with others lead to shared joy and practical care?
days.prayer: Lord, open Your word to us and make our joy generous.

days.context: After a decree threatens the Jews, Mordecai mourns and asks Esther to approach the king. Entering uninvited could cost her life, so she asks her people to fast before she acts.

devotional.title: Esther faces a dangerous choice
devotional.body: Mordecai's 'such a time as this' is a question about Esther's place in this particular crisis, not a promise that every risky action will succeed. Notice the community's mourning, Esther's danger, and her uncertain resolve.

days.observationQuestion: What risk does Esther describe, what does Mordecai ask, and how does she prepare?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might courage include listening to threatened people and acting with others?
days.prayer: Lord, give me wisdom and courage to stand with those in danger.

days.context: Job has suffered profound losses and argued with friends who wrongly insist that suffering proves his guilt. After Job's pleas, the Lord answers from the whirlwind with questions about creation.

devotional.title: The Lord answers Job
devotional.body: The speech widens Job's view of God's wisdom; it does not reveal a tidy reason for Job's losses. Do not use these questions to silence someone in pain. Read them after Job's lament and before the book's final correction of his friends.

days.observationQuestion: What parts of creation does the Lord ask Job to consider, and what knowledge is beyond Job?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might awe and honest lament be held together without pretending suffering is explained?
days.prayer: Creator Lord, meet those who suffer and teach me humility when I do not know why.

days.context: Psalm 23 portrays the Lord as shepherd and host. The speaker receives guidance and provision, walks through a dark valley, and trusts the Lord's presence even near enemies.

devotional.title: The Shepherd's care
devotional.body: The psalm does not promise a path without danger. Its comfort rests in the Shepherd who remains with the speaker through the valley and welcomes him to the table.

days.observationQuestion: Which images show care, and where does danger still appear within the psalm?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need the Shepherd's guidance or comfort?
days.prayer: Shepherding Lord, guide me and help me trust Your presence in the valley.

days.context: Psalm 51's heading places this prayer after Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba. David asks for mercy, cleansing, a renewed heart, and restored joy while acknowledging his sin.

devotional.title: Asking for a clean heart
devotional.body: The plea for forgiveness must not erase the harm done to Bathsheba or the consequences narrated in 2 Samuel 12. Repentance tells the truth and seeks changed conduct.

days.observationQuestion: What wrong does David confess, what renewal does he seek, and what kind of heart does God welcome?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need God's mercy and renewal?
days.prayer: Merciful God, make me truthful about my sin and ready to turn from harm.

days.context: Psalm 103 calls the soul to bless the Lord and remember His benefits. It praises forgiveness, compassion, steadfast love across generations, and God's knowledge of human frailty.

devotional.title: Remembering mercy
devotional.body: Read the praise as worship rooted in God's character, not a guarantee that every disease is removed immediately. The psalm itself remembers that human life is brief.

days.observationQuestion: What does the writer tell his soul to remember, and how is God's compassion described?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which of God's mercies do you want to remember today?
days.prayer: Compassionate Lord, keep me grateful for Your mercy and mindful of Your care.

days.context: Proverbs 3 addresses a learner with instruction about trust, generosity, wisdom, and the Lord's correction. It praises wisdom as more valuable than wealth.

devotional.title: Wisdom, trust, and correction
devotional.body: These are wisdom sayings shaping a life, not mechanical guarantees that faithful people avoid illness, loss, or crooked paths. Trusting the Lord involves humility about our own insight and care for neighbours.

days.observationQuestion: What actions are paired with trust in verses 1-12 and with neighbourly care later in the chapter?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where could humility or generosity make trust visible today?
days.prayer: Lord, guide my decisions and make me generous and teachable.

days.context: Ecclesiastes 3 names contrasting seasons of human life, reflects on God's timing, and urges people to receive work and enjoyment as gifts while acknowledging injustice and mortality.

devotional.title: Times we cannot control
devotional.body: A time for each event is not approval of every violent act or a promise that pain follows a neat timetable. The Teacher presses the limits of human control and the need to receive ordinary gifts.

days.observationQuestion: What contrasts are listed, and what questions about work, justice, and mortality follow?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could you receive one ordinary good without pretending to control its season?
days.prayer: Lord, grant me humility about time and gratitude for today's gifts.

days.context: Isaiah 9 speaks of light for people in darkness and a child associated with righteous rule. The chapter then turns to a repeated warning about judgment on Israel's pride and injustice.

devotional.title: Light amid judgment
devotional.body: Christians hear the royal child in relation to Jesus, but the promised reign should not be detached from Isaiah's setting or used to skip the chapter's warnings. Read both hope and judgment.

days.observationQuestion: What changes in verses 1-7, and what actions bring warning in the rest of the chapter?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the promise of just rule challenge the ways people misuse power?
days.prayer: Lord, give me hope in Your justice and ears for Your warning.

days.context: Isaiah 40 opens with comfort for God's people and announces a way prepared for the Lord. It contrasts fragile human life with God's enduring word and praises the Creator who strengthens the weary.

devotional.title: Comfort for a weary people
devotional.body: The chapter addresses a people in need of restoration, not a promise that every exhausted person will immediately feel strong. Notice how comfort is grounded in God's character and faithfulness.

days.observationQuestion: What reasons for comfort appear in verses 1-11 and 27-31?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where can you bring weariness to God without denying it?
days.prayer: Everlasting Lord, renew my trust as I wait for You.

days.context: Isaiah's Servant is rejected, bears others' iniquities, and is later vindicated. Read the chapter with the surrounding Servant passage in Isaiah 52:13-53:12 in view.

devotional.title: The suffering Servant
devotional.body: The poem links the Servant's suffering with the wrongdoing of others rather than celebrating suffering for its own sake. Christians read it in light of Jesus' death and resurrection (see Acts 8:32-35); that connection should be explained, not assumed or used to excuse harm.

days.observationQuestion: What does the passage say the Servant suffers, for whom, and what follows his suffering?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does the Servant's bearing of others' wrongdoing invite gratitude without asking the harmed to remain unsafe?
days.prayer: Lord, help me read the Servant's suffering with humility and hope.

days.context: Jeremiah speaks hope to Israel and Judah amid judgment and displacement. The chapter promises return, mourning turned toward joy, and a new covenant in which God's instruction is written on hearts.

devotional.title: Hope for a scattered people
devotional.body: The new covenant promise in verses 31-34 is addressed to the houses of Israel and Judah. Christian readers connect it with Jesus, but should not erase its first audience or treat restoration as instant relief for every sorrow.

days.observationQuestion: Who is promised a new covenant, and how does it differ from the broken covenant?
days.reflectionQuestion: How does God's commitment to forgive shape your hope without rushing grief?
days.prayer: Lord, make me attentive to Your faithful promise and forgiving mercy.

days.context: The poem speaks from affliction after Jerusalem's devastation. In the middle of grief it remembers the Lord's mercies, then returns to sorrow, injustice, and a plea for God to see.

devotional.title: Hope voiced within lament
devotional.body: The words about renewed mercy in verses 21-24 do not cancel the poem's pain. Read the whole chapter before using those verses to comfort someone else; lament and hope remain together here.

days.observationQuestion: What suffering is described before and after verses 21-24, and what does the writer ask God to see?
days.reflectionQuestion: Can you leave room for honest grief while recalling mercy?
days.prayer: Merciful Lord, see those who suffer and keep hope alive without silencing lament.

days.context: Ezekiel addresses Israel in exile. The Lord promises restoration, cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit, while explaining that He acts for the honour of His name.

devotional.title: A new heart for exiles
devotional.body: This is a promise to a displaced people within Israel's history, not a formula for claiming anyone else's land or a guarantee of immediate personal success. Notice that renewal includes a changed heart and life, not merely changed circumstances.

days.observationQuestion: What does the Lord say He will do in verses 22-27, and why does He say He acts?
days.reflectionQuestion: What kind of inward change is more important than outward success?
days.prayer: Lord, cleanse my heart and lead me toward faithful living.

days.context: Daniel's vision pictures violent beasts, the Ancient of Days judging, and one like a son of man receiving dominion. An angel later interprets the vision in relation to kingdoms and the holy ones.

devotional.title: The kingdoms and the court of heaven
devotional.body: The images are apocalyptic, not a code for confident predictions about today's leaders. Read the interpretation in verses 15-27 alongside the vision. Christian readers also hear Jesus' use of 'Son of Man' without flattening Daniel's whole scene.

days.observationQuestion: What do the beasts do, what happens in the heavenly court, and what does the interpretation say?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can God's final judgment sustain patient faith rather than speculation?
days.prayer: Lord, keep me faithful when earthly power appears overwhelming.

days.context: Hosea recalls the Lord calling Israel from Egypt and caring for the people, even as they turned to other gods. The chapter voices judgment and a striking refusal to give Israel up completely.

devotional.title: The Lord's compassion for Israel
devotional.body: The parental imagery expresses God's care for Israel within a troubled covenant relationship. Do not turn it into an assurance that wrongdoing has no consequences; notice the tension between judgment and compassion.

days.observationQuestion: What has the Lord done for Israel, how has Israel responded, and what does the Lord say about His compassion?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does this tension teach you about God's steadfast care?
days.prayer: Compassionate Lord, keep me from forgetting Your care or dismissing Your warning.

days.context: Amos laments for Israel and warns of judgment. The chapter calls people to seek the Lord, reject evil, establish justice in the gate, and stop treating religious festivals as a substitute for righteousness.

devotional.title: Seek the Lord and seek justice
devotional.body: The famous call for justice in verse 24 belongs to a concrete accusation against exploitation and corrupt worship. It is not merely a slogan for a cause; examine the chapter's concern for the poor and for honest judgment.

days.observationQuestion: What does Amos condemn in verses 10-13 and 21-24, and what does he call the people to do?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where might worship need to be matched by fairness toward a neighbour?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to seek You and to act justly.

days.context: Micah portrays a covenant dispute: the Lord recalls His saving acts, rejects the idea that extravagant offerings can replace faithfulness, and names justice, mercy, and humble walking with God.

devotional.title: What the Lord requires
devotional.body: Verse 8 belongs beside the charges of dishonest trade and violence later in the chapter. It is neither a way to earn rescue nor a vague call to be nice; it describes covenant faithfulness in public and personal life.

days.observationQuestion: What has the Lord done in verses 3-5, and what practices in verses 10-12 contradict verse 8?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which ordinary decision would better reflect justice, mercy, and humility?
days.prayer: Lord, help me walk humbly with You and deal honestly with others.

plans.title: Psalms for Prayer
plans.description: Twenty-one selected Psalms for praise, lament, confession, trust and thanksgiving.
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: 21 selected chapters, not every chapter of the Bible.
plans.purpose: To help you turn Scripture into prayer, trust, worship, and honest dependence on God.
plans.bestFor: Prayer, devotional reading, and reflection
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Psalm 1 opens the Psalter as a wisdom poem. It contrasts delight in the Lord's instruction with the way of the wicked, using a well-watered tree and windblown chaff as images.

devotional.title: Delight in God's word
devotional.body: The tree pictures a life rooted in God's teaching. Read the contrast as a wisdom portrait, not a guarantee that faithful people never suffer or that every project succeeds.

days.observationQuestion: What does the blessed person delight in, and how do the two images describe the contrasting ways?
days.reflectionQuestion: What would help you make room for God's instruction today?
days.prayer: Lord, give me delight in Your instruction and wisdom to walk in Your way.

days.context: Psalm 8 praises the Lord whose glory fills creation, then asks why He attends to human beings at all. Its answer gives humans dignity and responsibility within the created world.

devotional.title: Wonder and gratitude
devotional.body: The psalm does not make humanity the centre of worship. Human honour is received under God's majestic name, and care for creatures is a responsibility within His creation.

days.observationQuestion: How does the writer move from the heavens to humanity, and what is humanity entrusted to do?
days.reflectionQuestion: What in creation moves you to praise God?
days.prayer: Majestic Lord, teach me wonder at Your glory and care for what You have made.

days.context: Psalm 13 is a short prayer that begins with repeated 'How long?' questions, asks the Lord to answer amid fear of an enemy, and ends with trust in His steadfast love.

devotional.title: Bring the whole lament
devotional.body: The final note of trust does not erase the earlier distress. The psalm gives a worshipper room to name absence and fear before asking for help and recalling God's love. Follow its movement rather than forcing yourself to feel the ending immediately.

days.observationQuestion: What does the writer ask in verses 1-2, request in verses 3-4, and affirm in verses 5-6?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which part of this prayer gives honest words to your own situation today?
days.prayer: Lord, hear what I cannot resolve, and help me remember Your steadfast love.

days.context: Psalm 16 is a prayer of refuge. The speaker rejects rival gods, calls the Lord his chosen portion, and rejoices that God is before him and guides him in the path of life.

devotional.title: Finding refuge
devotional.body: Its confidence grows from belonging to the Lord rather than from controlling every circumstance. Christians also hear its hope in light of Peter's use of this psalm in Acts 2.

days.observationQuestion: What does the writer reject, what does he call his portion, and where does he locate lasting joy?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need to entrust your security to the Lord?
days.prayer: Lord, be my refuge and teach me to find joy in Your presence.

days.context: Psalm 19 first celebrates the heavens' witness to God's glory, then praises the Lord's instruction and ends with a prayer about hidden faults and acceptable speech.

devotional.title: Listening to God
devotional.body: The poem moves from creation to God's word to the worshipper's own life. Let each part speak before choosing only one favourite line for prayer.

days.observationQuestion: What do the heavens declare, how is God's instruction described, and what does the writer ask at the end?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which words of this Psalm can become your prayer?
days.prayer: Lord, open my eyes to Your works and word, and guard my speech and heart.

days.context: Psalm 23 portrays the Lord as shepherd and host. The speaker receives guidance and provision, walks through a dark valley, and trusts the Lord's presence even near enemies.

devotional.title: The Shepherd's care
devotional.body: The psalm does not promise a path without danger. Its comfort rests in the Shepherd who remains with the speaker through the valley and welcomes him to the table.

days.observationQuestion: Which images show care, and where does danger still appear within the psalm?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need the Shepherd's guidance or comfort?
days.prayer: Shepherding Lord, guide me and help me trust Your presence in the valley.

days.context: Psalm 27 opens with confidence in the Lord as light and salvation, yet also contains pleas for help and a final call to wait. Threats and hope appear in the same prayer.

devotional.title: Courage while waiting
devotional.body: The writer's confidence does not cancel his request that God hear and answer. Read both halves to let courage and dependence remain together.

days.observationQuestion: What does the writer declare in verses 1-6, ask in verses 7-12, and urge in verses 13-14?
days.reflectionQuestion: What fear can you bring into God's presence?
days.prayer: Lord, hear my plea and strengthen my heart as I wait for You.

days.context: Psalm 32 celebrates forgiveness after the writer stops concealing sin. It moves from the weight of silence to confession, release, instruction, and a call for the upright to rejoice.

devotional.title: Confession and forgiveness
devotional.body: Confession is honest naming of wrong, not a way to erase consequences for people harmed. The psalm's joy arises from the Lord's forgiving mercy.

days.observationQuestion: What changes when the writer acknowledges wrongdoing, and what guidance follows?
days.reflectionQuestion: What do you need to confess rather than keep hidden?
days.prayer: Merciful Lord, give me honesty to confess and wisdom to repair harm where I can.

days.context: Psalm 42 voices longing for God while the writer remembers former worship and hears the question, 'Where is your God?' Its repeated refrain speaks to a downcast soul.

devotional.title: Longing for God
devotional.body: The refrain does not shame sadness or make it vanish at once. Thirst, tears, memory, turmoil, and hope all remain part of this prayer.

days.observationQuestion: What causes the writer's longing, and how does the refrain answer his downcast soul?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can this Psalm give words to your longing?
days.prayer: Lord, hear my longing and keep me turned toward You while I am unsettled.

days.context: Psalm 46 calls God a refuge amid shaking earth and raging nations. It pictures God's presence with His city and calls hearers to behold His work, including the ending of war.

devotional.title: Refuge amid trouble
devotional.body: The call to be still comes in a poem about God's rule over upheaval and conflict. It is more than advice to relax; it asks worshippers to acknowledge His sovereignty.

days.observationQuestion: What troubles are named, what does the refrain repeat, and what does God make cease?
days.reflectionQuestion: What trouble do you need to place before God?
days.prayer: God of refuge, hold me steady and teach me to trust Your rule amid trouble.

days.context: Psalm 51's heading places this prayer after Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba. David asks for mercy, cleansing, a renewed heart, and restored joy while acknowledging his sin.

devotional.title: Asking for a clean heart
devotional.body: The plea for forgiveness must not erase the harm done to Bathsheba or the consequences narrated in 2 Samuel 12. Repentance tells the truth and seeks changed conduct.

days.observationQuestion: What wrong does David confess, what renewal does he seek, and what kind of heart does God welcome?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where do you need God's mercy and renewal?
days.prayer: Merciful God, make me truthful about my sin and ready to turn from harm.

days.context: Psalm 63's heading locates David in Judah's wilderness. Thirst becomes an image for seeking God; the writer recalls worship, praises God's steadfast love, and rests in His help.

devotional.title: Seeking God
devotional.body: This is a prayer of longing in scarcity, not a claim that worship removes every physical need. Attend to how remembering God sustains praise in the wilderness.

days.observationQuestion: What images of need appear, and how does the writer remember and bless the Lord?
days.reflectionQuestion: What competes for the attention you want to give to God?
days.prayer: Lord, meet me in my need and keep my desire turned toward You.

days.context: Asaph is troubled by the apparent prosperity of the wicked. His view changes when he enters God's sanctuary and reflects on their end and on God as his portion.

devotional.title: Envy brought into worship
devotional.body: The psalm does not deny that injustice can look rewarding. It records a struggle, a turn in perspective, and a renewed confession of nearness to God. Read the change in verses 16-17 in the light of the whole poem.

days.observationQuestion: What troubled the writer at first, what changes in the sanctuary, and what does he say is good in verse 28?
days.reflectionQuestion: Where can you bring comparison or injustice before God without pretending it is simple?
days.prayer: Lord, receive my confusion and teach me to seek Your nearness.

days.context: Psalm 84 is a song of longing for the Lord's dwelling place. It blesses those who dwell there and pictures pilgrims whose strength is in God as they journey toward worship.

devotional.title: Longing for God's presence
devotional.body: The psalm's longing is communal and connected to the place of worship, not merely a private wish for a calmer day. Notice the journey as well as the destination.

days.observationQuestion: Who is called blessed, what happens along the journey, and what is the writer's deepest desire?
days.reflectionQuestion: What helps you seek God in an ordinary day?
days.prayer: Lord, deepen my longing for Your presence and strengthen Your people on the way.

days.context: Psalm 90 contrasts God's enduring life with human brevity. The prayer names mortality and trouble, then asks for wisdom to number our days, mercy, joy, and enduring work.

devotional.title: Wisdom with our days
devotional.body: Numbering our days is not a technique for avoiding death. It is a request for wise life before the eternal God, with honest attention to frailty and a plea for His compassion.

days.observationQuestion: What contrasts are drawn between God and human life, and what does the prayer ask for?
days.reflectionQuestion: How could you use the time entrusted to you wisely?
days.prayer: Eternal Lord, teach me wise use of my days and establish what is good.

days.context: Psalm 95 begins with a communal invitation to praise the Creator and Shepherd, then calls worshippers to hear His voice and warns against hardening their hearts as Israel did in the wilderness.

devotional.title: Praise and hear
devotional.body: The warning is part of this worship psalm, not an interruption to discard. Praise and attentive obedience belong together. Notice the shift at 'Today' before turning the opening lines into your own prayer.

days.observationQuestion: What reasons for worship appear in verses 1-7, and what warning follows?
days.reflectionQuestion: How might worship today include listening and responding as well as singing?
days.prayer: Lord, receive my praise and keep my heart open to Your word today.

days.context: Psalm 103 calls the soul to bless the Lord and remember His benefits. It praises forgiveness, compassion, steadfast love across generations, and God's knowledge of human frailty.

devotional.title: Remembering mercy
devotional.body: Read the praise as worship rooted in God's character, not a guarantee that every disease is removed immediately. The psalm itself remembers that human life is brief.

days.observationQuestion: What does the writer tell his soul to remember, and how is God's compassion described?
days.reflectionQuestion: Which of God's mercies do you want to remember today?
days.prayer: Compassionate Lord, keep me grateful for Your mercy and mindful of Your care.

days.context: Psalm 121 is a song of ascents that lifts a question about help toward the hills and answers that help comes from the Maker of heaven and earth, who does not sleep.

devotional.title: Looking for help
devotional.body: The repeated language of keeping expresses deep trust in the Lord. Do not turn this pilgrim song into a prediction that believers can never be injured on a journey.

days.observationQuestion: Where does the writer say help comes from, and what does the psalm repeat about the Lord's care?
days.reflectionQuestion: What need can you entrust to the Lord's care?
days.prayer: Maker of heaven and earth, keep my trust in You as I travel through this day.

days.context: This song of ascents begins with a cry from the depths, asks who could stand if the Lord kept account of sins, and turns to forgiveness, waiting, and a call for Israel to hope.

devotional.title: From the depths to hope
devotional.body: The writer does not claim that waiting is easy. Forgiveness gives reason for reverence, and hope rests in the Lord's steadfast love and redemption. Let the personal cry and the final communal invitation both shape your prayer.

days.observationQuestion: How does the prayer move from verses 1-4 to waiting in verses 5-6 and hope for Israel in verses 7-8?
days.reflectionQuestion: What does waiting with hope look like when you cannot hurry an answer?
days.prayer: Lord, hear my cry, forgive me, and teach me to wait on Your mercy.

days.context: Psalm 139 praises God's searching knowledge and presence, reflects on life formed by Him, then includes a fierce plea against the wicked before asking God to search the writer's heart.

devotional.title: Known by God
devotional.body: Do not skip the difficult anger in verses 19-22 or turn it into permission to harm an enemy. Let the final request for self-examination test the way you pray the whole psalm.

days.observationQuestion: How does the writer describe God's knowledge and presence, and how does the final prayer follow the difficult verses?
days.reflectionQuestion: What would you like to ask God to search and guide in you?
days.prayer: Searching God, know my heart, confront what is harmful, and lead me in Your way.

days.context: Psalm 150 closes the Psalter with repeated calls to praise the Lord. It names His mighty acts and greatness, calls for many instruments, and invites every breathing creature to join.

devotional.title: Let everything praise
devotional.body: The final psalm is a communal doxology, not a private rule about musical style. Its wide invitation turns attention from the worshipper's preference to God's worthiness.

days.observationQuestion: Why is praise offered, where is it voiced, and who is invited to join?
days.reflectionQuestion: How can you express gratitude and praise today?
days.prayer: Lord, receive the praise of all who have breath for Your mighty works.

plans.title: New Testament in 1 Year
plans.description: One chapter at a time, with reflection days spread throughout the year.
plans.pace: One chapter or a reflection reading daily
plans.estimatedTime: About 5–10 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: All 260 chapters, with 105 reflection days distributed across the year.
plans.purpose: To help you stay with one Bible book long enough to notice its flow and message.
plans.bestFor: Slow book-by-book reading
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Matthew is one of the four Gospels, presenting Jesus' identity, teaching, kingdom mission, death, and resurrection. Read this book with attention to its own portrait of Christ, while remembering that every episode serves the larger witness to who Jesus is.

devotional.title: Following Jesus in Matthew
devotional.body: Matthew presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Matthew reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.

days.context: This reflection day returns to Matthew 1 so the passage can settle rather than simply be checked off. Read it again in its book context, watching for repeated words, commands, promises, warnings, and what the passage reveals about the Lord before moving to application.

devotional.title: Return to Matthew 1
devotional.body: A slower reading can reveal what a first reading missed. Come back to the passage with attention to repeated words, commands, promises, warnings, and the way it points you toward God. Let review become meditation, not busywork.

days.observationQuestion: What did you notice this time that you did not notice before?
days.reflectionQuestion: What part of this passage needs to shape your trust, repentance, worship, or obedience today?
days.prayer: Lord, help Your Word remain with me and form me in faithful love for You.
days.gentleAction: Write one sentence you want to carry from this passage today.

plans.title: Old and New Testament Daily Pairing
plans.description: Read both testaments every day, with occasional New Testament rereadings for reflection.
plans.estimatedTime: About 10–20 minutes reading; allow another 5–10 for reflection. Longer chapters may take more time.
plans.coverage: Every Old and New Testament chapter across 365 days. Some New Testament chapters are revisited to keep both testaments present each day.
plans.purpose: Read both testaments every day, with occasional New Testament rereadings for reflection.
plans.bestFor: Long-term whole Bible reading
plans.rhythm: Read the passage, use any guidance provided, reflect and pray, then complete the day when you are ready.

days.context: Matthew is one of the four Gospels, presenting Jesus' identity, teaching, kingdom mission, death, and resurrection. Read this book with attention to its own portrait of Christ, while remembering that every episode serves the larger witness to who Jesus is.

devotional.title: Following Jesus in Matthew
devotional.body: Matthew presents the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Read with your eyes on who He is, what He reveals about the Father, how He brings the kingdom, and how He calls people to trust and follow Him.

days.reflectionPrompt: What does Matthew reveal about Jesus that should shape your faith today?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, help me see You clearly and follow You faithfully.

days.context: Acts follows Luke's Gospel and shows the risen Jesus continuing His mission by the Holy Spirit through His witnesses. The gospel moves from Jerusalem toward the nations through preaching, prayer, suffering, repentance, and Spirit-formed community.

devotional.title: The risen Christ at work
devotional.body: Acts shows the risen Jesus continuing His mission by the Spirit through His witnesses. Watch how prayer, courage, suffering, preaching, repentance, and community form the early church as the gospel moves outward.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Acts show the Spirit empowering witness to Jesus?
days.prayerPrompt: Risen Lord, make me faithful by Your Spirit in ordinary witness and love.

days.context: Romans belongs to Paul's apostolic letters, written to churches or coworkers with gospel truth for real belief, worship, holiness, endurance, and shared life. Read commands and encouragements from the foundation of grace in Christ, not as detached religious advice.

devotional.title: Reading Romans as gospel-shaped instruction
devotional.body: Romans is part of Paul's apostolic teaching for churches and believers. Look for how gospel truth leads into worship, identity, holiness, unity, endurance, and love. Keep grace as the root, not merely behavior as the goal.

days.reflectionPrompt: How does Romans connect what God has done in Christ with how believers now live?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, let Your grace take root in my belief, worship, relationships, and obedience.

days.context: Hebrews belongs to the General Epistles, writings that strengthen believers in endurance, truth, holiness, love, discernment, and hope. Read its correction and comfort as words for God's people learning to remain faithful under pressure.

devotional.title: Receiving Hebrews
devotional.body: Hebrews helps believers endure, discern truth, love faithfully, and live as God's people. Read for both comfort and correction, remembering that Christian obedience grows from belonging to the Lord.

days.reflectionPrompt: What comfort or correction does Hebrews bring to faithful discipleship?
days.prayerPrompt: Lord, strengthen me to receive Your word and live faithfully as one who belongs to You.

devotional.title: The Lamb reigns

days.prayerPrompt: Lord Jesus, keep my hope fixed on Your victory and coming renewal.
